1.	Has the dominion bureau of statistics, since the outbreak of the present war, made any revisions in the method of determining the cost-of-living index?
2.	In the determining of the cost-of-living index, are the following factors taken into consideration, (a) deterioration in quality of goods available; (b) indirect increases in cost of living resulting from that amount of increased taxation being used to subsidize certain lines of consumer goods; (c) disappearance of certain lines of consumer goods from the market; (d) the virtual disappearance of so-called bargains and special prices?
3.	Is the dominion bureau of statistics completely independent from the wartime prices and trade board in its work in connection with the determining of the cost-of-living index?

1.	The present cost-of-living index replaced the bureau's index on the base 1926=100 in August, 1940. This new record covers the period commencing January, 1935 and extending to the present time. No change in method has occurred since August, 1940, although two revisions in the index budget have been made. In January, 1941 several items were added to the budget, and in February,, 1943 further adjustments were made to take account of wartime changes in consumption. These are considered in detail in a published memorandum entitled "Revised Explanation and Description of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics Cost-of-Living Index". From July, 1942 onward, additional taxes on cigarettes and tobacco have been excluded from indexes calculated for the purpose of
Questions

reckoning cost-of-living bonuses by instruction of order in council P.C. 6219 as amended.
2.	(a) For many years the bureau has asked stores reporting clothing and home furnishings prices to report estimates of quality changes in addition to changes in price. A reported decrease in quality of 5 per cent is treated exactly the same as a price increase of 5 per cent.
(b)	The cost-of-living index measures changes in the cost of a budget of goods and services from month to month. Indirect taxes, with the exception of tobacco noted above, are included since they form a part of the actual price paid by the consumer. Direct taxes are not included in the cost-of-living budget since they do not change the consumer price of budget items.
(c)	As already indicated, certain adjustments in the index budget have been made resulting from the disappearance of consumer goods from the market. The full cost of such items has been distributed among other similar budget items in the same group, so that this operation results in no reduction of the index. Movements in the index continue to reflect only the influence of price changes upon the cost of the index budget.
(d)	The cost-of-living index has always been based entirely upon regular selling prices.
3.	The Dominion Bureau of Statistics is accountable solely to the Minister of Trade and Commerce for work connected1 with the cost-of-living index, as for all other work which it does.

FUNDS HELD IN TRUST FOR INDIANS
speechtext:
1.	Has a letter been issued by the superintendent of Indian agencies at Regina, notifying the Indians that only part of the interest accruing from money held in trust will be paid to the Indians during the war?
2.	If so, what is the reason for such action, and upon what authority is it based?
3.	Is this policy being adopted with reference to all Indians living on reservations in Canada?

subtopic: FUNDS HELD IN TRUST FOR INDIANS
speechtext:
1.	No. An attempt has, however, been made through inspectors and Indian agents to persuade Indians to forgo temporarily, in whole or in part, the distribution of interest earnings and other moneys held in trust for them.
2.	The earning power of the Indians generally is much higher than normal. Opportunities for gainful employment are the best in many years. Demand for Indian labour in all industries, and particularly in agriculture, lumbering and fishing, is strong. On the Pacific coast the restriction placed on the Japanese has created an unprecedented

demand for Indian labour in the fishing fleet and factories. Lumber camps welcome all Indian labour they can get. On the prairies Indian camps are combed for all available farm labour. Lumber and wood camps, farms and fishing stations readily absorb all Indian labour they can get. Fur prices are better than they have been in the past two decades. The army and other forces have accepted a great many of the Indians and pay and allowances to dependents are far above the normal Indian living standard. Crops have been good and prices for grain fair and for 'live stock produced on reserves better than average. It is considered sound policy in times of relative prosperity and urgent need for the full utilization of manpower and high wages to provide against a day of possibly greater Indian need and to that end to encourage the saving of the unearned income of the bands.
The representatives of the bands have been consulted, local conditions and local needs examined and considered. Many bands have voluntarily consented to the deferment or curtailment of annual distribution of their unearned income. Some have voluntarily offered to invest it, or a substantial part of it, in war savings certificates. Many bands, where local conditions or contractual obligations warrant it, have been paid in full.
3.	Yes.

subsubtopic: LOSS OF PERSONNEL THROUGH SINKING OF SHIP IN NORTH ATLANTIC
speechtext:
I have been in receipt of communications from a number of members of this house and from people outside with reference to rumours regarding the recent loss
of a number of members of the Royal Canadian Air Force by the sinking of a ship in the north Atlantic, and I desire to make the following statement on the facts.
The vessel in question was a ship of British registry of 8,862 tons, designed for peace-time carriage of both passengers and freight, and having a speed of fifteen knots. She carried a crew of 86 and the passenger accommodation consisted of 12 two-berth rooms with bath, and 29 other berths, providing cabin accommodation for 53 passengers. She was fitted with lifeboat capacity for 231 and travelled in naval convoy.
Under the recently revised regulations agreed to by the United States authorities, the joint United Kingdom and United States shipping board, the Admiralty, the Air Ministry and the Canadian authorities, a vessel of this description travelling in convoy is permitted to embark as crew and passengers a maximum of seventy-five per cent of the lifeboat capacity. The lifeboat capacity as stated above was 231, seventy-five per cent of which is 173. Personnel on board consisted of the crew of 86, and R.C.A.F. personnel numbering 53, a total of 139, well within the prescribed limits.
Because of the superior type of available passenger accommodation, the speed of the ship and the provision of naval convoy, the offer of the entire available space to the R.C.A.F. was immediately accepted. Rumours to the effect that this was a slow freighter not suitable for passenger accommodation are, of course, not in accord with the facts. Every precaution was taken to safeguard the lives of these gallant young men. It should be pointed out that on account of the serious shipping shortage every available berth on such ships must be used, and had the space not been taken up by the R.C.A.F., officers of other arms of the services would have been placed on board. It should also be stated again that the submarine is still the enemy's most powerful weapon and that the battle of the Atlantic is not yet won. Any ocean trip to-day in any part of the world is fraught with danger and I think I may safely say that our record in transporting our soldiers and airmen to the United Kingdom is one of which we may all be proud.
No one deplores more than I do the loss of thirty-seven of the finest of our young men, who gave their lives for their country as surely as if they had done so in actual combat with the enemy, and I extend my deepest sympathy to their loved ones in their bereavement.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: TRIBUTES TO HER LATE MAJESTY AND THE BRITISH COMMONWEALTH OF NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the
House of Commons on this twenty-fourth day of May might appropriately and profitably take time for a moment to pay tribute to a greatly beloved monarch of yesterday, the late Queen Victoria, and at the same time do homage to that great empire with which her name has always been affectionately associated, the British commonwealth of nations.
In the last great war the British empire came out of that severe testing period with colours flying high. In the second great war the empire is emulating successfully its achievements of the past. Its colours still fly high and I think that this house may appropriately at this time pause and pay a well-merited tribute to the British commonwealth of nations and all that it stands for in the realm of freedom and righteousness.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: TRIBUTES TO HER LATE MAJESTY AND THE BRITISH COMMONWEALTH OF NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) that it is very fitting that to-day a tribute should be paid not only to the memory of the great Queen Victoria but also, as he has said, to the British commonwealth of nations. I can think of no greater tribute that could be paid than that which is being paid to-day by the armed forces of Canada in the part which they are taking in this great war for freedom, by the part which is being taken by the men and women in our various war industries and by the people of Canada generally in all that pertains to the war effort. The magnificent response which was recently made to the victory loan indicates how deeply the people of Canada have at heart all that relates to the preservation of liberty and freedom. Certainly no reign in history was more identified with the obtaining of many of the liberties we enjoy to-day than that of Queen Victoria.
I thank my hon. friend for having risen to recall to the memory of all present what we owe to so great a sovereign, remembering in this particular the queen's illustrious great-grandson, our present king. If I may be permitted to make the suggestion it would I think be most fitting for hon. members to rise and join in singing the national anthem on this Victoria Day.
(The members rose and sang the national anthem.)

subtopic: MESSAGE OF APPRECIATION FROM DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER OF GREAT BRITAIN

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MESSAGE OF APPRECIATION FROM DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER OF GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Saturday of last week the Right Hon. Clement R. Attlee, Deputy Prime Minister of Great Britain and Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs, sent a telegram to me as Prime Minister of Canada in reference to the passage of the Mutual Aid bill.
This communication was, I understand, given out in London either on Saturday or yesterday. It has appeared in some of the press of Canada this morning. It is fitting, however, that it should have its place on the records of parliament and I shall accordingly read the communication.
It is dated London, May 22, 1943, and reads:
From the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs.
To the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
The following for your prime minister (begins):
On the occasion of the passage of the Mutual Aid bill through its final stage, I wish to express to you the gratitude and admiration ot the people and the government of the United Kingdom for this magnificent contribution.
When last year the government of Canada made a gift of a thousand million dollars to the United Kingdom, Mr. Churchill spoke of it as [DOT]being unequalled in the whole history of the British empire. Canada has herself now surpassed her previous contribution. By this measure and by steps she has taken to purchase interests of government of the United Kingdom in Canadian munition factories and to assume financial responsibility for R.C.A.F. squadrons, Canada has provided means for Britain and other members of the united nations to obtain from her a continued flow of war supplies to the value of over $1,800 million. These unselfish and far-sighted measures have not only added immeasurably to common reserves in fighting for freedom but have prevented accumulation of ivar debt which would be a burden on prosperity of the world in years to come.
Canada's role as an arsenal and storehouse has become ever more important as the war progresses. The supplies furnished by Canada under billion dollar gift were a powerful factor in the success of the Eighth Army. Now that the day is coming for the final assault on the enemy, the new supplies now to be made available will enable Canada's strength and power to be felt all over the world.
I ask you therefore to accept this expression of the deep appreciation of His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom for a statesmanlike gesture which affords a most hopeful augury not only for accomplishment of the present task but also for the development of future understanding between nations on secure and lasting foundation.
C. R. Attlee.

The Late William Aberhart

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the Minister of Justice. In view of the announcement over the week-end that the Third International had been dissolved, will the minister state to the house whether the government has given consideration to giving the communist party in Canada legal status?
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice):	Mr. Speaker, if I understand the
hon. member's question he wishes to know whether, in view of the declaration made in Russia on Saturday the government had given consideration to giving legal status to the communist party in Canada. There has been no opportunity for the government to consider that matter since the announcement was made. I might point out to the hon. member that it would probably require both the deletion of a regulation in the defence of Canada regulations and an amendment to the criminal code to give legal status in Canada to any party that might advocate the overthrow of the existing institutions by means of force. It struck me when I read the declaration that it perhaps made it unnecessary now to give any further consideration to section 39(c) of the defence of Canada regulations, which was passed at a time when the communist party of Canada formed part of the Communist International. If that organization has now been dissolved and the group in Canada which formed part of it follows the recommendation which the newspapers have reported as having been made by the Comintern, there would no longer be any useful purpose in referring to the matter. It would be an organization that had disappeared, and it would be of no interest to anyone w'hether or not it remained banned. If any other party or group should be made up of men who formerly belonged to this organization, it would depend upon the attitude they adopted as to whether or not any further action should be taken with respect to them.

speechtext: On the orders of -the day:

subtopic: REFERENCES TO DEATH OF PREMIER OF ALBERTA
speechtext:
I should like to refer to an occurrence which took place since we last met. Since this house adjourned on Friday last an event occurred which to hundreds of thousands whom I have the honour to represent has come as a tragedy. Social Crediters everywhere, as well as all people sincerely interested in reform, heard with the deepest regret of the death of Premier William Aberhart of Alberta. Even those who for various reasons opposed the famous monetary reform leader have felt the loss to our generation of a man so able, so sincere, so public spirited, so courageous and energetic as was the dynamic Alberta premier. Upon the request of the press yesterday I issued the following statement, which I ask the indulgence of the house to read into the record:
In the passing of William Aberhart a great man has gone, a great man with a great message. He was an ardent Britisher, a tireless advocate of the principles of true British democracy. Of the leading statesmen of his time, some spoke of freedom from want and fear; some promised it; he alone pointed the way by which, without loss of individual liberty, such freedom from want and fear can be attained. He lighted a light that men must not allow to be put out.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REFERENCES TO DEATH OF PREMIER OF ALBERTA
speechtext:
May I say to my hon.
friend who has just spoken that before he rose I received a note from my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Gray-don) asking me if I thought I should make a reference to the passing of the late Mr. Aberhart. The thought had occurred to me [DOT] before I came into the house, but in seeking for precedents as to references to the passing of provincial premiers, I have been unable to discover any, and it seemed to me that the general tradition of confining references of the kind to members or ex-members of the federal parliament or to personages who have held very high position was perhaps the one to which I should adhere. For that reason alone I made no reference to the passing of Mr. The Late William Aberhart

Aberhart, the late Premier of Alberta, in whom we all recognized one who played a great part in the affairs of his own province; one who, from the point of view of my hon. friend and his followers, deserved, I am sure, the encomiums which have been expressed by the leader of the Social Credit group. My. hon. friend will realizie that while we all, I think, respected Mr. Aberhart and had a high opinion of not a few of his qualities, there are many of us who did not agree with some of the measures and doctrines he advocated, and for that reason might not be expected to express ourselves in reference to his public services in quite the same terms as have been used by one who was a devoted disciple and follower.
I hope the hon. gentleman will feel that I speak on behalf of hon. members of this house when I express the desire that our sympathy should be conveyed to Mrs. Aberhart and the members of the family in the bereavement they have sustained. I join very sincerely with my hon. friend not only in expressing sympathy to those who have been so greatly bereaved but, so far as I am individually concerned, in expressing a sense of personal loss in the passing of one who was a friend, though a friend with whom I differed considerably in matters of policy.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REFERENCES TO DEATH OF PREMIER OF ALBERTA
speechtext: I should like to add just a word to what has been said in reference to the deceased premier of the province of Alberta. In my opinion Mr. Aberhart's passing will be mourned by a great section of this country, for three reasons in particular. First, whatever may have been the differences among people with respect to their social, economic or political views, Mr. Aberhart was a Christian gentleman who by his example did a great deal for public life in Canada. In addition, he was an enthusiastic pioneer in social and economic reform. Then perhaps it is particularly appropriate on this 24th day of May that it should be said also that, the premier of Alberta was a staunch supporter and earnest devotee of all the principles and ideals of the British commonwealth of nations which we have commemorated this afternoon. Therefore I join with the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) in expressing to the widow and family our very deep sympathy in their bereavement.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, May 21, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to bis majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley- Mr. Bradette in the chair.

This being May 24,
Mr. Chairman, and fitting reference having been made in this house to the British commonwealth of nations, may I add that I am sure the conference which took place last week in Washington will go down in history as a gathering of great national and international importance; I believe the future will prove the truth of this statement. I am sure all hon. members join with me in welcoming back the Minister of National Defence after his participation in that great gathering.
Last Tuesday, just before the minister left, I was quoting from the Winnipeg Free Press in reference to medical practitioners and the No. 3 casualty clearing station. At that time I was not sure of the date of the article, but since then I have checked it up and find the date to be April 28, 1943.
Now I should like to say a word with respect to dependents' allowances, for I think some amendments should be made and some improvements brought about in this connection. I have a letter dealing with a case which I have discussed from time to time with the parties interested; this is not an isolated case by any means, and I should like to quote a paragraph from the letter in order to bring out the point more clearly:
In this case the husband , deserted the wife some time prior to his enlistment, and when she endeavoured to have a warrant served upon him under the Deserted Wives' Maintenance Act the police were unable to find him, so that the [DOT]warrant was never served.
He proceeded overseas and since he has been there his wife has been refused maintenance because maintenance is being paid to a woman with whom he was living in Winnipeg prior to his departure overseas.
While I can understand the regulation of the dependents' allowance board that no allowance will be granted to a wife who is living apart from her husband and he has not contributed, if in a financial position so to do, in the six months preceding enlistment, I cannot understand a regulation which permits the payment by a husband so deserting his wife, to another woman whom he decides to leave his wife to live with. This seems to put the onus on the wrong party-if anyone has to establish the right surely it should be upon the husband to prove his wife is no longer as deserving as the

War Appropriation-Army
mistress whom he has replaced her with. It outrages both my sense of decency and my pocket as a taxpayer that this woman should be denied an allowance in such circumstances.
This case has been discussed before, both in the house and' in committee, and I suggest it should be cleared up.
Another matter I would mention has to do with children sixteen years of age. I believe when they attain that age they are no longer permitted to receive dependent's allowances. Where it can be shown that they are continuing their education, and making progress in that regard, in my opinion assistance should be continued for another year or two, until they have reached the age of seventeen or eighteen years. I trust that some provision will be made in this respect.
When the minister spoke he said there were several items with which he had not time to deal. I would refer however to transportation, a subject which is causing many people considerable concern. They are not sure, nor are their representatives in this chamber, that all this transportation of armed forces is necessary. Certainly it creates a great congestion of traffic. I suggest the minister should state what the' transportation costs have been in Canada in the past year. I realize that in respect of certain specialized training, when training centres are located at different points across the country, it is necessary to move the troops back and forth so that they may obtain the required training. I doubt, however, whether it is necessary to the extent it now obtains, and I believe there has been considerable waste effort in this respect. Let me give one example-and it is not an isolated example by any means. A young chap whose home is in a city not far from here was home on leave, and while there applied to his officer commanding, in Vancouver, for an extension. The extension was refused. He reported back to Vancouver, only to be informed immediately that he was to proceed to a training area near Toronto. I have known many such instances, and it seems to me this condition could be checked, thereby preventing a great amount of unnecessary travel. I would ask the minister to explain whether it is essential to have this constant movement of armed forces back and forth across the country, because, apart from the cost entailed, it certainly does congest traffic.
I had intended to say something about man-power, but I assume that subject will be dealt with in detail by some other hon. members; and further, I do not wish to take more time of the committee just now.

Mr. Chairman, my first words on rising to take part in this discussion will be words of congratulation to the Minister of National Defence upon the very clear and precise statement he gave the committee. He has had a terrific task. Canada's peace-time army of 4,500 has grown to a war-time army, with all the various ramifications demanded by modern warfare, numbering 450,000 men. This has been indeed a terrific undertaking. Had it not been for his organizing and executive ability I doubt if such accomplishment could have been possible. No man charged with the responsibility of carrying out any part of Canada's war effort has had a greater task to perform, and no one has done it better than the Minister of National Defence.
During his remarks he referred to the Dieppe raid. A number of hon. members who have followed him in the debate have made similar references most of which however have been critical. I do not intend to discuss the raid in great detail, but I shall refer to it briefly. Truly it cannot be said to have been a great military victory, but it was a great feat performed by armed forces, so far as the planning and carrying out of plans, the courage and devotion to duty, and- the self-sacrifice of those who took part in the raid were concerned. The loved ones of the heroes of Dieppe must take great comfort from the fact that much valuable information was obtained from the raid, information which will be invaluable in the days to come when the armies of all the united nations attack the shores of France.
Would not the information obtained be of equal value to Germany?

Well, I do not know how it could apply to Germany. The information was obtained by Canadian troops for the benefit of the troops of the united nations. I have no doubt the united nations have gained much benefit from the raid. My point is that the loved ones of those who gave their lives in that raid will derive great comfort from the fact that many others will now be enabled to raid the continent, go on to victory and come back in safety to their loved ones in Canada.
In reporting upon the raid, the Minister of National Defence held nothing back. He told our people what had taken place, and the casualties which had resulted therefrom. In this connection I refer to a Canadian Press dispatch bearing a New York date line, and appearing in the Brantford Expositor. I have

War Appropriation-Army

ao doubt the same dispatch appeared in many other dailies across Canada. The article is headed, "No Sugared Report on Dieppe Raid", and states:
New York, September 24. The New York Daily Mirror, tabloid morning newspaper, editorially complimented Canada to-day for the frankness of defence minister Ralston's report on the Canadian-led Dieppe operation last month. . . .
Captioned "Canadians get no bunk, no evasions," the editorial said: . . .
The people of Canada got no sugared report, bluntly, Defence Minister Ralston announced that the 5,000 Canadians who made up five-sixths of the raiding forces suffered 67 per cent casualties, killed, wounded and missing. . . .
In short the story of Dieppe, as it was told by the government of Canada to the people of Canada accomplished these strengthening results:
1.	The people of Canada accepted their casualties because the necessity for casualties was explained.
2.	The people of Canada were taken "inside" the story of Dieppe; though they were separated from the fighting front by the width of the Atlantic, they were brought to the ringside of a battle fought largely by Canadians.
3.	The people of Canada were reinforced in their belief that their government does not permit any admirals or generals to cover up or twist the details of "costly" operations.
Here, in America, we can learn mueh from Canada's example. . . .
Canada had to show us the way to price control. Now Canada shows us the way to fighting morale.
I place that on record so that we may recall that with respect to Dieppe we were told about the casualties, we were told the cost, and we were told something of the great results obtained. I am confident that in respect of future operations the Minister of National Defence will keep the house and country advised of the part Canada is playing.
In his statement the minister gave us figures showing the number of men now in the army. They total approximately 450.000. Of' this number, 190,000 are abroad. These men have been waiting in England; they are eager to fight and yet they have been restrained for the last three years. They have had a splendid record in England. It is not an easy thing for an army to wait and wait and wait. Canada's army are well trained and this country is more prepared to-day than she ever was to strike a blow when the time comes. I should like to read an excerpt from an article which appeared in the London Daily Sketch and which I feel pays a well-deserved compliment to Canada. It reads: Ready and Waiting
The Canadians like England and Wales, and love Scotland, but it is no good telling them they are doing a grand job in defending these islands. Their reply is they are not concerned so much with defence as with smashing the Hun and getting back home.
[Mr. W. R. Macdonald.1
Then the article goes on:
Their morale has not suffered during the long wait; they are keen, smart and training hard.
And again:
They are extremely well behaved, and the cases one sometimes reads about are the exceptions to the rule.
The article then goes on to refer to the fact that only one man a week 'out of 16,000 is brought before the magistrate's court, and it continues:
Do you know of any town of 16,000 population that has only one police case a week, or a city of 100,000 inhabitants that has only six a week?
To my mind that is a great compliment to the men in England who have been waiting all these months for the day and the hour in which to attack. A short time ago an hon. member of this house, discussing reinforcements, stated that the number of reinforcements for Canada's army was not more than ten or twelve per cent. That hon. member did not know what he was talking about; nevertheless his statement appeared in the press from one end of the country to the other. What are the facts? The minister has stated that at the present time there are
190,000	Canadians in England. This force is made up of five divisions. If we estimate the number of men in a division as 15,000, the five divisions would total 75,000. Then let us say there are 25,000 men in the divisional corps and acting as army troops. Over and above the men in the army and those 25,000 who belong to the divisional corps and are acting as army troops, there are still 90,000 trained men in England. So that in England alone there are reinforcements to the extent of ninety per cent.
But that is not the whole story. The minister has told us that at the present time there are 80,000 men in training in Canada. These men are rapidly being trained to take their places with the men in England. If we add these 80,000 men to the ninety per cent which we have in England, instead of having only ten or twelve per cent reinforcements we find that we have to-day reinforcements to the extent of 170 per cent. I submit that reinforcements to that extent are ample and should give confidence to those whose loved ones are abroad. They will know that there are many men ready to take the place of those who first go into battle.
The minister told us that the total number of men in Canada is approximately 240,000. I have referred to the 80,000 who are in training to be sent abroad. There are 80,000 who are in the home establishments, that is, men who are in the training centres. I should like to pay a tribute to these men in the

War Appropriation-Army
training centres. There is a training centre known as No. 20, near Brantford. I have watched this training centre grow up and I know something of the spirit of the men. I can say that the officer commanding and the other officers take a keen interest in every man in the training centre. I can say the same for the non-commissioned officers and other instructors. There is a great spirit in this training centre; they feel that they have a job to do. I think what can be said for No. 20 can be said for the other training centres throughout Canada.
Then there are 80,000 other troops who are to be used for home defence. I take it that the sixth, seventh and eighth divisions are part of this 80.000. It recently came to my attention that the men belonging to the sixth, seventh and eighth divisions in Canada are now wearing patches of different colours on their sleeves. I remember when in the last war the custom was established of putting patches on the sleeves of the men in order to distinguish them in battle. Every one knows that in the heat of battle the various divisions and brigades and regiments get mixed up and these patches were used so that a man could distinguish those who belonged to his battalion, and to make it easier for the battalion to get together. It came to be looked upon as a battle honour. It was a distinction for the man who had really served in the line of battle. What do we find to-day? We find that these home defence division's which will probably never be in battle as divisions are distinguished by these patches. Recently I read an article in the Globe and Mail, written by Ralph Allen, a man who had served in the ranks of the Canadian army for a number of years. He received his discharge from the army and has been writing some most interesting articles on the life of the soldier in England. Word of these patches has reached England and the men over there are greatly dissatisfied to know that the patch is no longer a battle badge, but is simply something to be worn by members of the forces no matter where they may be.
Another unfair feature about the wearing of these patches is the fact that there are many hundreds of men in Canada who have volunteered for active service but who do not belong to any particular division. These men are being trained; they would like to go abroad and probably they will go abroad some day, but in the meantime they do not belong to any division; therefore they wear no patches. I think it would bring about an improvement in the morale of the Canadian troops if no patches were worn by the men, 72537-1881
no matter' to what division they might belong unless they have been in an overseas division.
As I said before, the minister stated that there are approximately 80.000 men on home defence. In other words, these men are defending Canada from the shores of Canada. I realize that we must have defensive forces in Labrador, in Newfoundland, in Nova Scotia and along the Pacific coast line. However, it does seem to me that 80,000 men are, under present circumstances, more than enough for this purpose. I know that many young Canadians who have not volunteered for service abroad are just as patriotic, just as loyal and love Canada just as much as those whc have gone abroad. Most of these young men would willingly give their lives for their country: they would fight to the death for Canada. Unfortunately many of them are under the impression that this is not Canada's war but that it is Britain's war, and that we are fighting to help somebody else and not to help ourselves.	.
Not now, surely.

Of course that view is entirely wrong. The armies that drove the axis forces from North Africa did just as much to save Canada as they did to save North Africa itself. Just because we are further removed from the actual place of conflict does not mean that we are likely in case of defeat to escape the horrors and terrorism of nazi domination. I have always believed' and still believe that the only way to keep war from Canada's shores is to send men abroad to seek out Hitler in lands far from Canada and fight nazism wherever it can be found. This is Canada's war just as much as it is Britain's war or the war of any of the united nations. Make no mistake about it, Canada is fighting for her very existence.
Under the provisions of the National Resources Mobilization Act, every young man called for military training is being trained in Canada to fight anywhere in the world, and by a stroke of the pen he can be required to go anywhere in the world. However, as long as we have an ample force of men who have volunteered to fight abroad there is no point in forcing others to go who, in the very nature of things, would not be as good soldiers as those who have volunteered. Nevertheless I have no doubt that if our armies abroad require reinforcements, every man in the army in Canada who is physically fit and properly trained will be sent abroad for that purpose. Until that day comes, and if our home defence force is to be increased beyond 80,000, at which number
War Appropriation-Army

it now stands, I suggest to the minister that draftees who will not volunteer to serve abroad' should be sent in ever-increasing numbers to Alaska to defend Canada from that corner of the country. By a recent order in council, draftees can be sent to Alaska and to Newfoundland and other places adjacent to Canada. At the present time Alaska is being defended to a large extent by soldiers of the United States. If Canada sent her draftees there, the United States soldiers could be relieved to fight in other parts of the world, and we would be cooperating with them in the best interests of the cause for which we fight.
The minister in his statement referred to the future of our army. He gave the house the number that would be required for the army in the year to come. At that time he stated that it would probably not be necessary in the future to produce certain equipment which Canada is now producing. I am quite in accord with him.; in fact I mentioned such a 'contingency when speaking in this chamber last year. On June 19, 1942, as reported in. Hansard, page 3501, I stated:
No doubt at the present time we have a greater need of munitions than of men, but with the ever-increasing output in Canada, and more particularly in the United States, and with the ever-changing ebb and flow of battle it is possible that within a comparatively short time we may need men to fight with the munitions rather than men to make the munitions.
When this war started it was stated that Canada would probably become the arsenal of the united nations. That is a great ambition, a great goal towards which to strive. But, Mr. Chairman, there is something greater than being the arsenal of the nations. To my mind it is much greater to provide the fighting men to fight with the equipment which is made in the arsenals. Canada has played a great part as an arsenal, but as the war progresses we are going to need men in the army more than we ever needed them. The day is fast coming when the arsenals of Canada will slacken in their output, and at that time the forces of Canada must increase. The minister has stated that 700,000 men is not an excessive army for Canada. To my mind it is far from an excessive number. We can have an army in Canada of many more than seven hundred thousand. Those men will come as the years go by. To-day more than ever before we need an all-out war effort, not only in the arsenals of our country, but to keep up our army and to increase its numbers.
Let me however at this time suggest to the minister that if men are coming from the war industries to the army it might be possible to transfer some of them from the war industries to the farms. I am not one of those who

believe in cutting down our armed forces indiscriminately in order to take men for this job and for that job. After all, it is the army that is going to win the war. True, the army must be fed and equipped, but with all the food and equipment you cannot win a war unless you have a well-trained army. Yet, we need food, and our farmers must have help. I suggest to the minister that when men are being released from the war industries, a proportion, not necessarily large but as many as can be spared, should be sent to the farms to assist in producing the food which the workers and the soldiers, sailors and airmen must have.
At the present time men are granted leave to assist farmers with seeding. This leave was granted on or about May 5. Ten days have elapsed since these men were sent home to assist on the farms. What are the conditions on the farms? We have had almost continuous rain. In most parts of Canada it has been impossible to get on with the seeding. These men have been home ten days and the seeding is not done. Probably twenty days of their leave remain, but they cannot complete the seeding in that time. I therefore suggest to the minister that all men who have been granted leave for seeding should have that leave extended, because it is a fact that the farmers cannot get their seeding done in the remaining twenty days which are left for the men who are on leave.
I would make another suggestion. I am not a farmer and do not profess to know anything about farming, apart from the fact that I know that seed is put in about this time of year, that late in June and early in July the hay must be taken off, and that hardly has the hay been taken off before the harvest is ready to be garnered. County councils throughout the province of Ontario have passed resolutions requesting that men who are given leave should not merely receive four weeks' leave to do seeding, then go back to their regiments, and then in say six weeks have another six weeks' leave to help with harvesting. After due inquiry has been made and it has been established that these men are needed on the farms, would it not be better to give them three or four months' continuous leave so that the farmer could get all his work done and would not worry, when he got his seeding done, how he was going to get his haying off, and when he got his haying off he would not worry how he was going to get his harvest in.

In the course of the debate the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) referred to the provisions now being made for men returning from the front. Last year several acts were passed by this house with regard to men returning from the present war. There was an act giving the right to those who had served on the farm*

to return to the farms and to receive substantial benefits. They are to be reestablished on the farms. Another act was passed to enable them to take up their old employment. It required employers to reestablish them in their former employment if that was in existence. Another act was passed, a general rehabilitation measure.
This government is taking great interest in the returned men, as both it and all other governments have taken in the men who returned from the last war, and it should be a matter of some satisfaction to members of the committee to know that pensions paid to Canadians are higher than those paid to the men who have served with any other army. In Canada the widow of an ex-service man killed in action receives, if her husband was a private, the sum of S720 a year; in New Zealand she would receive $281.39; and in the United States $456. This goes to show that this country tries to be fair to those whose loved one did not come back, as well as to those who did but who had suffered some disablement. It is true you can never repay a man for offering his life and for suffering for his country. What we can do is to try to put him in a position to compete with his fellow workmen in Canada when he returns from his service abroad. I am confident, Mr. Chairman, that as this war goes on more measures will be brought down which will be of benefit to those who have offered their all to save their country.
In conclusion I would say to the Minister of National Defence that the people of Canada have confidence in his leadership. They feel that he is directing the armies of this country along the paths which will enable them to play their part when the day comes for final victory.

Mr. Chairman, I shall not endeavour to follow the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald), who has just taken his seat. This afternoon I intend to deal with only one subject, namely, the matter of man-power as I see it, not only in reference to reinforcements for our army overseas but in regard also to the allocation of the necessary man-power for industry and agriculture.
I listened to the minister as he made his statement, and I have read and reread the speech he delivered, and I do not think I overstate it, Mr. Chairman, when I say it is apparent to anyone reading between the
.Mr. W. R. Macdonald.]
lines of his statement that the minister realizes the tremendous difficulty that faces the government of this country in securing reinforcements for the army overseas and the proper allocation of man-power for agriculture and industry in Canada. I am going to read just one portion of the minister's statement. At page 2664, after setting out the purpose we all have in mind, namely, the defeat of the axis, the minister said:
To accomplish this, our job has been and is, and will be-because it is far from over yet-(a) to organize and maintain the strongest force of which we are capable, well forward in the main theatre of operations, for use wherever Germany and Italy can be met and overcome; (b) to cooperate in the defence of North America ...
And finally:
. . . preserving a vitally important source of supply to the Canadian army here and overseas and to the united nations of raw material, foodstuffs and ammunition.
With these three items I intend to deal this afternoon. Let me say at this stage that while the hon. member for Brantford City found no difficulty in being able to assure the people of Canada that the necessary reinforcements for the Canadian army overseas are available, he had to resort to speculation, and finally to computation based upon speculation, to arrive at that conclusion. What we on this side of the house ask for, and I think we have a right to demand it on the part of the people of Canada, is 'clear and definite information on tfie subject of the adequacy of reinforcements for the army overseas. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White) and the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) have dealt with various phases of this question. That is not the phase I am going to deal with in particular this afternoon, but rather the general problem- of man-power, which cannot be discussed piecemeal.
Although this house has been in session now for over three and a half months, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) as yet has been unable to place before parliament and the country the situation with respect to man-power. That responsibility rests upon him and no one else. In the discussions which have taken place here within the last

I have here two issues of "Canada at War", May, 1943, dealing with man-power, and February, 1943, dealing with man-power, and they are identical in wording:
"Responsibility for mobilizing and allocating all man-power in Canada rests with national selective service, under the Department of Labour. All departments concerned, such as the Department of Munitions and Supply, Agriculture and the armed forces, are cooperating."
The minister has stated that the war is far from over, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has stated that the united nations now face their supreme hour. We are in a different position at this stage of the war from the position we were in during the last war, because our casualties so far, comparatively speaking, are small, amounting to 5,786 as of April last. I think the experience and the victories of recent days, and the fact that we have been assured over and -over again during the last three years that the necessary man-power is available, have resulted in the people being less disturbed than they should be over the man-power situation. There has been little sacrifice yet except in the families of those who have given their sons. In spite of the fact'that we have been more than three and a half years at war, the production of luxuries, which should be at an end, is still being continued. After three and a half months in session this parliament has yet to learn whether the government has a plan for the allocation of man-power. The Prime Minister dealt with this matter on March 24, 1942, and set out the situation with respect to man-power at that time. Now, one year later, and we are still in the same position. There is no man or woman in Canada to-day other than the government itself,-and sometimes I doubt whether the government has a plan-who can say what the man-power plan is for Canada. Having regard to conditions, I accept as my thesis these words, that the man-power issue must be faced by this parliament; and whether or not it will be popular from the point of view of votes, it will have to be settled." We in this house must take stock of the man-power situation; for our outstanding problem is to assure the necessary men for the armed services while at the same time retaining indispensable men in industry and

Expedients effective for a short while have been brought in from time to time. I suggest that the government should do away with this policy-what I choose to call a nibble-nibble policy-and bring in a comprehensive one which will attack the problem forthrightly. The time is past when palliatives can be administered to avoid cures, and when continuing postponement of necessary action can take the place of decisions. I believe hon. members of the committee recognize, and it' is axiomatic to say, that in this country no man should be the master of his choice of service in our war effort or of the decision as to where and when he will serve.
I said a while ago that there was no agreement among the ministers. I shall not go in to this in detail at the moment, except to quote what two of the ministers have recently stated. The Minister of Munitions and Supply is reported to have said at page 2622 of Hansard of May 13. He said:
. . . but I would point out that there is a very serious over-all shortage of man-power in war industry to-day. I know of very few plants that have the number of men required to permit them to obtain the desired output.
On May 18, as reported at page 2765 of Hansard, the Minister of National Defence said this:
I should think that there would be a shrinkage, as time goes on, in the requirements for men in industry, particularly war industry.
And a little later on:
-but I should think this new condition would be bound to make it possible to undertake comb-outs of men who in the past have been postponed because they were essential in war industry, and in addition, it should release men from the non-essential industries.
I asked the minister for his plan in that regard. The question I asked was this, as reported at the same page.

Mr. Ralston: No, I have not. That is not a figure I would have; it would be a matter for my colleague, the Minister of Labour.
Certainly there is no agreement between the statement of the Minister of Munitions and Supply and that of the Minister of National Defence. A moment ago the Minister of National Defence asked me where I got my figures with regard to the needs of industry. In September, 1942, a document issued by the bureau of information indicated that there were 2,000.000 persons employed in nonessential industries in Canada; that there were
1,250,000	workers on farms, and 1,200,000 workers in essential utilities and mining. The total number of persons in Canada between 'the ages of 14 and 65 years was estimated to be 7,000,000. Brought up to date, this means that Canada has less than fifty per cent of her available man and woman-power mobilized as compared with some sixty-six per cent in Great Britain. Some will say that

there is a shortage of man-power, but I do not believe that there is a man-power shortage in Canada.
When I get a chance to make a speech on man-power I think the hon. member will find that the figures I will put before the house will not be so far behind those of Great Britain.

I say that it is the fault of selective service, which cannot act efficiently under the powers it has to place man-power where it should be placed. Instead of a nibble-nibble policy of interfering with a few trades and occupations during the past month, it is necessary in the interests of national survival that we administer this problem with equality from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I repeat that there is not a shortage of man-power to-day, but there is a shortage, and I quote, of "the right labour, in the right place, at the right time."'
During the past few days we have heard it said that we are short of manpower, but in answer to that argument I would refer to a statement made by Mr. W. J. Couper, executive assistant to the deputy minister of labour. Speaking in Toronto on April 13, 1943, he is reported to have said:
An increase of 250,000 to 350,000 workers in Canada will be required within the fiscal year ending March 31 next, and present employment in non-essential industry will be curtailed to the extent of some 200,000 workers by the end of that period.
Then follow these words, which I think indict the government as has no other man in the service of the Department of Labour to the present time:
We are suffering a labour shortage now because we don't have the right labour in the right place at the right time.
And again:
In the efficient utilization of labour, this is supposed to be rationed between employers and the armed services, but the former are not experienced in dealing with national emploj'ment service and similar lack of experience obtains for employees. . . . The national employment service machine begins to creak from time to time.
That is the story of the executive assistant of the deputy minister of labour who gave his explanation of what has happened.

What does a motor car
do when it goes uphill? It begins to creak.

It is more likely to
rattle going down.

In connection with industry I shall not go into details except to say that lumber production is far below the
