war needs of the nation because of a shortage of some 46,000 men who ought to have been allocated by the national selective service to this work. Our railways are operating to-day with fewer men than ever before and yet are handling greatly increased freight and passenger traffic. In April, 1943, our railways were operating with sixteen per cent less manpower than they had at the outbreak of the war. Their revenues were some forty per cent more than at the outbreak of the war and yet national selective service are calling up experienced men from the railways and sending them into the armed services of the country with the result that the railways will be forced to recruit green men to take the place of those removed from the transportation systems and placed in the army.
For the past year opposition members have been trying to tell the government the real situation in connection with coal production. It was pointed out that there would be a national calamity in this regard and little regard was given thereto. In May, 1943, the minister was given tremendous powers and the Prime Minister admitted we are to-day faced with one of the greatest emergencies in this regard in our history. Was there any allocation of men during the past year for the cutting of wood? One could not get men in western Canada to go into the bush to cut wood because wages had been fixed in 1941 at a time when wood cutting was just casual work undertaken by homesteaders and the like.
Recently there was an article in the press which indicated a lack of coordination and cooperation between the departments of government. This article showed that an automobile plant manufacturing a front-line vehicle was recently short 1,000 men while at the same time private machine shops and machine shop workers in Winnipeg were idle, and this at a time when naval escort vessels were required to be built. I might add that one of the leading men in the press gallery wrote an article in the Winnipeg Free Press within recent months stating that the objectives of selective service have not been reached, that employment offices have not tried to direct labour to the proper war industries but have issued permits letting labour go where it pleases, and the closing down of non-essential industries has not been followed.
To-day the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) received an answer to a question asked of the Minister of Munitions and Supply. He asked if contracts had been cancelled for the production of certain guns and other war materials. I shall not give the details of these because they will appear in Hansard. In answering the question to-day the minister,
after saying that military information cannot be divulged since it would not be in the public interest, quotes with approval his own statement, as reported in Hansard, at page 2708.
I do hope that there will be no further speculations of the kind contained in the article. Announcements will be made as soon as the facts of the situation can be determined.
The information is denied, although in a United States magazine published in Washington, it is stated that there is to be a reduction in ground war production and some of the munitions and guns mentioned in the question asked by the hon. gentleman are referred to. "When that reduction takes place, thousands of men will be out of employment. What assurance can the minister and the government give that these men will not be hoarded in any one industry, that they will be transferred into some other industry immediately a closing down or a reduction of manpower becomes necessary in the industries in which they are working? For, unless something is done now, and unless the selective service administration is stopped creaking, we shall have an unemployment condition which will have most serious effects when regard is had to the necessity of war production being kept to high levels.
I am not going to pursue this matter further, except to make some suggestions. As far as we on this side of the house are concerned we have at all times advocated the effective total utilization and the proper allocation of man-power for war, by compulsion where necessary. The government has decided this month that compulsion is necessary in order effectively to allocate labour in certain designated industries. It brought in compulsion for military service in Canada. It has gone that far in enacting compulsion. I was astonished at the import of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Brantford City, that in the interests of cooperation Canada should take those who are called up for service and send them to Alaska, so that Americans, who fight in all parts of the world, should be relieved for the purpose of fighting. I thought that was a most peculiar proposition to advance in the interests of amity as between these two nations.
What about the call-up system? I am not, going to deal with it at any length to-day except to say this, that under the present system there is no equality of administration or equality of enforcement everywhere throughout Canada. As a matter of fact, under the National Resources Mobilization Act. while the government in the reports issued in "Canada at War" would indicate that there is equality of sacrifice, that about 2-9 per cent of those eligible for call are
War Appropriation-Army

called up, everywhere in Canada, they do not reveal the true facts, in that the percentage is based upon the number of men there were in 1939 and the national increase which has taken place since, without deduct ing from the figures the numbers of men who have enlisted for overseas service. I ask the minister, why were these particulars of enlistments removed from "Canada at War"? On page 20 of the January issue full particulars of the intake of the armed forces were shown. In the month of February the same information was given. I took it upon myself in February last to analyse these figures. In the issues of March, April and May no reference is made to the numbers of men enlisting, the numbers who are called, or the proportion of those who actually answer the call. Why are these facts omitted?
The great criticism I have of the National Resources Mobilization Act is that it is conscription masquerading as voluntaryism. Men are forced to voluntarily enlist thereunder, and the result is that there is no selectivity. Fear of the draft forces into the armed services many men-mechanics, coal miners and others-who are needed in Canada, and who, if the selective system were carried into effect, would be kept at their respective occupations. Men must be directed into the place where they will render the best service, otherwise the condition in which industrial life finds itself to-day through the shortage of man-power will grow worse with the passage of time, and we shall find ourselves with insufficient men on the farms of this country, insufficient men in industries in the right place at the right time, insufficient men in the armed forces of this country and due to failure of selective service to allocate man-power.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has now spoken for over forty minutes.

I have just a few remarks to make in this debate, in which I have not yet taken part.
In the first place I will read a letter, which is in French, but I will summarize it afterwards. My correspondence is very extensive, and it comes from all over the province of Quebec and from many parts of the country. But here is a letter which I have received tom Black Lake, Megantic county: {Translation) Dear Sir,
I am writing to you in the hope that you may help my son who is at present in the camp at Farnham; he has been there two months; re was arrested while in hospital where he

had just undergone a surgical operation; he had not fully recovered; the doctor had ordered a treatment which the officers forbade, claiming that he was well enough.
(Text) It is a young fellow who was sick and who underwent an operation. He had to follow treatment afterwards, but the army doctors at the camp told him not to follow it, that he was well.
(Translation) On the very next day he was ordered to scrub the floor of the clink and had to sleep on the floor after an operation; this was not very pleasant.
(Text) The following day they forced him to wash the floors of his cell, and they ordered him to lie on the floor. After an operation that is not very funny.
(Translation) Besides, sir, he had a discharge from the active army in his pocket when he was arrested at the hospital; the officers have taken it and now they will not admit having done so.
(Text) He had a discharge from the active army in his pocket. They took it from him and they did not give it back.
(Translation) He had enlisted twice at the Saint-Jacques recruiting office, in Montreal, but hail failed to pass the physical test and had been given a discharge. I fail to see why they keep him in the reserve army while sick.
(Text) He went twice to enlist at St. James street. Montreal. He did not pass, and he had his discharge.
(Translation) The doctor had told him that he would have to be operated on for liver trouble; he has had no treatment since; they give him nothing but laxatives. He has been in the clink for two months and is about to be transferred to a detention camp. I have been told that you alone could prevent him from going there; he must not go to a detention camp in his state of health. You would be rendering us a great favour if you were good enough to take this matter up. My son's name is . . .
The name appears in the letter.
(Translation) I have not told you why he has been arrested; it is because he. left the reserve army on account of his bad health. His discharge paper was taken from him at the Quebec citadel. If you are unable to help him, let us know. Thank you.
(Text) I think it can be summarized this way: that fellow went to enlist in the active army and was found unfit; then he was accepted in the reserve army, stayed home to undergo an operation, and before he had completely recovered they came and got him and forced him to wash the floor.
I appreciate many things which the hon. member for Lake Centre has said. He has spoken without any partisan spirit. I congratulate him upon this; it is the only way to take up such matters before the committee. I intend to show no political bias

War Appropriation-Army
of any kind. I want, first, just to state facts and explain to the committee the situation with regard to farmers, and a little later I will take up the case of the army doctors.
I will confine myself to farming. In the first place, it is useless for members to rise and ask questions on this matter if it is taken for granted that all men of military age who are physically fit should be in the army. If that stand is taken we might just as well stop the discussion immediately. But in my humble view there are certain occupations that are essential to the war effort and also to the welfare of the community, and those occupations require men who are physically fit and young. Agriculture is one of these occupations and railroading is another. As I said a year ago, it is impossible to expect young men to come from the Lady Grey hospital in Ottawa and work as firemen or brakemen on the railways, and it is equally impossible for such men to engage in agriculture. If the minister does not admit that agriculture is an essential occupation I will discontinue my remarks at once, but I know he will not say that. He cannot say that agriculture is not an essential industry.
Going through my correspondence, I find a letter which I received from a well educated lady of the eastern townships who married a lawyer. He dropped his legal practice, however, to take up farming. This letter is dated April 30. I will not mention the lady's name, but I can give it to anyone who asks for it. I am prepared to give the first page of her letter. I quote:
Huntingdon, Que.,
April 30, 1943.
.T. F. Pouliot, Esq.. M.P.,
Riviere du Loup, P.Q.
Dear Sir:
I believe that you may be interested in knowing what is the situation in this part of Quebec and enclose herewith copy of letter I have written to Mr. Ladouceur, director of national selective service at Valleyfield, situated about 20 miles from our farm.
I have read with considerable interest your efforts to get parliament to deal with the pressing matters of interest to the ordinary man and farmers of this country.
I have been getting Hansard and read it. I must say it is both grim and amusing.
She used to be on the Hansard staff, but I pass that over.
My husband took leave of absence from his law practice in Toronto early in summer of 1914 to assist his parents who were old and in difficulty. War broke out and he never was able to rid himself of responsibility. He became active in cooperatives, organized Montreal Milk Producers Association, built up a pure bred Holstein herd, becoming president of Holstein Association of Canada, etc.
We have always had plenty of grief with the help problem but in 1940-41 it became desperate with enlistments and call-ups. Our herdsman got a job as inspector when military camp was built at $7 a day then a job of tire chief at a munition plant at $3,000 a year. . . . Finally we had a sale in September, 1941, some purchasers being Senator Raymond, Hon. F. Leduc, Hon. Geo. S. Henry, Macdonald college, etc. Dr. J. E. Lattimer stated that this herd was the highest producing per cow at the lowest cost per gallon of all herds in cost of milk survey.
But we had no alternative but to sell out as we could get no assurance of help. Our course has been justified as things have gone from bad to worse, as per letter enclosed.
Now listen to this:
Agriculture faces ruin under price ceilings, lack of labour and confiscation of profits under income tax law. Farmers will not expand operations only to get a penalty instead of reserve for old age, replacements, etc. All our fences are down from ice and snow and the fields are strewn with shingles blown from the barn during hurricanes of last winter. Our neighbour's barn collapsed from weight of snow and ice.
This is a pretty sad story, and it comes from one who has a practical knowledge of farming and who knows the circumstances. She sent me at the same time a copy of a letter from the selective service man in Valleyfield. I will keep that until the labour estimates are under consideration. What I have given, however, is sufficient to show the distress of agriculture at the present time, and farmers are asked to do more at this very time. This is something I cannot understand. The minister has given certain figures, but to me it is inconceivable that men should be taken from the farms in large numbers and that we should expect the work to go on just as well. I have read statistics that were tabled by cabinet ministers on Friday last and there is one bit of information that is missing. That is the number of farmers' sons and farm help who are in training camps in Canada and in the army on both this side and on the other side of the Atlantic, and elsewhere. We want to know the number of such men. We do not want percentages. I do not believe in decimals and fractions in connection with matters of this sort. I should like to know the number of farmers in the army, in various training camps both in Canada and outside.
This is not the first time that I have spoken on this subject. I suggest that selective service should have been established long ago. It came much too late. Indeed, I had to fight and fight very hard to have the idea of selective service acted upon. I have been told that once the selective service receive requisitions from the Department of National Defence, those requisitions have to be filled.
War Appropriation-Army

wouldn't bo much as reply to five other letters we have written to him since. We even enlisted the cooperation of agronomist Rinfret, who went to the trouble of writing in our behalf, hut with no more success than we'd had. That's the unaccountable part of it.
Could you not suggest some one else to whom we might write or could you not personally lend us a hand, for you are the only one from whom we have not yet sought assistance.
Our letters to the commanding officer were in two instances accompanied by a medical certificate definitely attesting my utter unfitness for service. I have over fifty arpents under cultivation, 4 cows, a team of horses, 3 calves, a breeding sow and 3 ewes. It's a foregone conclusion that unless I can get my boy's help to put in the crop this spring, I shall have to give up the land and go destitute together with my whole family. You can well imagine that in our present plight my boy's help is absolutely indispensable to me.
I should be most grateful to you for any help you may give us in securing this exemption we have so long endeavoured to obtain.
We shall take pleasure in supplying you with any particulars you may require, and trust we may hear from you in this regard.
(Text) This fellow complains that there is some propaganda to give the farmers the idea that they are well looked after. I do not entirely blame the Department of Labour or the national selective service, but I say that in the army things are going very badly so far as the farmers are concerned. There are no experts on agriculture in the army, andi they have the idea that- it is the duty of a young man to be not on the farm but in the army, that he should not be on the farm unless he is unfit for military service. That is the view of Captain Andrews, in particular, and later I intend to speak about him. The people of this country have been fooled by that propaganda, after all the trouble we took in explaining to national selective service andi the army the distinctions that should be made. In the opinion of the army as long as a man has been to camp, even if he has not had any-training at all, he comes under the Department of National Defence. If he is a farmer he must watch out; it will be very hard for him to get out, even if he is badly needed at home. Then here is a letter from the county of Laprairie:
(Translation)
Sir,	.
Though a stranger to you, I am a Canadian and the father of eight children, two of whom are in the army. . . .
This man has two boys in the army.
. . . and Mr. Maxime Raymond managed to obtain for one of them a six weeks' leave to help my brother who farms 138 arpents of land and who needs him the year round. You are under a serious handicap when, after deciding to cultivate a big garden you lose your hired help before the planting is done. We immediately sent another request to his commanding officer and we arc anxious about the 
reply. I have made up my mind to ask your assistance, after reading an article published in Le Devoir of March 5, 1943, in which the minister of the selective service said, in a letter addressed to you, that a draftee would be given three months in order to find employment on a farm. My son does not have to look for employment; on the contrary, my brother Adrien, a farmer at St. Jacques le Mineur, whose children are still too young to help him, w-ishes to hire my son who has always worked on farms and has as much experience as any real farmer, because he was born and brought up on a farm up to the age of 21, and he is now 25 years old. If you need more information, kindly get in touch with Mr. . .	.
Other young men from around here have obtained postponements for an indefinite period, while my son got but six weeks. When he obtained his leave, he was at the Rideau military hospital, Ottawa, his regimental number was . . . ; he was under Major Dunlop's orders who required that all our requests be written in English. We complied with his wishes and see what we obtained. He is the only one from around here who is in that position; how-ever, according to the newspapers and the answers that are given you on the floor of the house, the orders in council are not to that effect.
Trusting you -will suffer this little sacrifice in my behalf, I remain,
Yours admiringly,
(Text) This man has a son who was an experienced! man on. the farm. Now his brother is alone on that big farm and cannot get any help. He wanted his nephew to help him, but- all he was able to get was six weeks' leave, which was not enough. Moreover, the commanding officer insisted on the request being made in the English language. He did not consider a request made in French, so that the man put his request into English, but I do not know if he succeeded in getting what he wanted. I place this case before the minister and the committee.
I have before me another letter from Bona-venture county; these are only samples I am reading. I have to work from nine o'clock in the morning until twelve o'clock at night to read all these letters. I cannot read them all now, but I must point out to the committee that the plight of agriculture in Quebec is real; it is not exaggerated.. If it is not remedied by the army as well as by national selective service, we shall face famine next winter. No food for our armies in Canada, no food for our civilian population, and no food for export to our allies outside Canada, across the seas, would be a serious matter.
Once I had the privilege of listening to a very fine speech over the radio in which it was said that food does not grow on the shelves of a grocery store, but that it grows on the land. Food comes from the farmer, and it is because I do not want anybody to

War Appropriation-Army
suffer from famine or from hunger that I am insisting upon this point. I hope the minister will give careful consideration to what has been said.
This is what is said by another gentleman from Duret, Bonaventure county:
(Translation) Dear Sir,
I am writing to you concerning my son Gelasse in order to secure for him a six months' postponement. Last year I asked for such a postponement on his behalf so that he might work on my farm. I am a farmer and have no other son. I am sixty-five years old and unable to work. Last year the application for postponement was rejected. I have been able to put in only half of the crop. My son was in training at Valcartier and he himself came to do whatever small harvesting I had to do. He did not return to his camp since last summer. Once the harvest had been completed, he was taken ill and was attended by Dr. Paul Lacroix of Port Daniel Station. He is not yet well enough to return to his camp. If you wish to know exactly to what extent he has been ill you may get in touch with Dr. Paul Lacroix. I am asking a six months' postponement for my son so that I may put in and harvest my crop. Last year I did only half the work. I have a large farm and he is my only son. His regimental number is . . .
(Text) I can, show this letter to the minister. In this instance the young man went to help his father who has a big farm. While so helping his father, he became ill, had to be attended by a doctor and) then could; not return to camp. He wants ah extension.
I was saying a moment ago that the farmers have been deceived by the publicity and propaganda broadcast with respect to the orders in council of March of last year in connection with selective service. No exception was made with regard to leaves or postponements for farmers. What farmer can make a distinction between a postponement and a leave? It means the same thing to him. It is immaterial to him whether he obtains a postponement or a leave, so long as he is permitted to remain on the farm. They are not familiar with the technical language. They know their own business well. In one respect they are technicians; but they are not technicians, as writers. They do not split hairs, because they have no time for that, having something more important to do.
The greatest publicity was given the provision exempting farmers. I was in Toronto the day after, and I saw published in every paper the big headlines stating that farmers were exempted from training. Farmers stayed at home, on the understanding that they were exempt, and did not have to go. When they received notice to report they thought it was a joke, or something like an April fool prank. Their reply was, "We saw it in the newspapers. We heard over the radio that all farmers were exempted, because agriculture is an essential industry. Why should we go for further exemption, and be subjected to red tape, when we are already exempted?"
There is no more sensible man than the Canadian farmer, and that was the kind of reasoning he did. The propaganda and publicity were for the purpose of making farmers believe they were exempt; otherwise that would not have been the way it was done. Over the radio and in the press no distinction was made with regard to national selective service, and the Department of National Defence. I appeal to the memories of hon. members now listening to me; it was something to relieve the farmers' minds, before the plebiscite. It was just political propaganda, and I denounce it bitterly. It was done in order to induce the farmers to vote "yes" on the plebiscite, and that is the only reason why it was there. That is the charge I have made against the Minister of National Defence, who did not dare to put the plebiscite question as it should have been put.
I did not put the question.

The question was, are you for or against conscription for overseas? and in order to induce farmers to vote "yes" on the question as it was put, orders in council were passed-and they were in effect three days before they were published. I am sure the Minister of Justice has not forgotten the correspondence we had on that point.

I do not know what my hon. friend is talking about. I did not frame the question for the plebiscite, and had nothing to do with the passing of the orders in council, except as a member of the government.

I will explain what I have said. What I have said was that the Minister of National Defence did not have the guts to say to the Canadian people that the question was, are you in favour of or against conscription, yes or no?
The Minister of National Defence was not framing the question at all- and the Minister of National Defence takes no second place to the hon. member in the matter of guts.

That is right; the Minister rises, and I am glad he does so. But what I said-and what I repeat-is that the Minister of National Defence made several speeches, and did not say anywhere to anyone, not even to his constituents, "The question is, are you for or against conscription for overseas?"
War Appropriation-Army
I put the question as the question was framed; that is how I put it.
And it meant nothing.
A lot of people in Canada thought it meant something.

I am glad the minister has risen like this. It is a good thing for him to
speak, because finally he will admit something.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; the hon. member has spoken for forty minutes.
I beg your pardon, Mr. Chairman; I have been interrupted by the minister. I should like to speak for another forty minutes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The interruptions do
not entitle the hon. member to speak again, because he did not even take his seat while they were made. He would have the right to speak again, after he has taken his seat.

As I listened to the hon.
member for Lake Centre I was struck, as usual, with his vehemence and his earnestness, and also by the amount of his research into booklets and his perusal of letters in order to make the speech he made this afternoon.
As I listened to him I thought that had I never heard him before, with his voice, his head and his finger carrying conviction, as a new listener I would have felt the British commonwealth and the allied nations were trembling in the balance, and that in particular his majesty's government in Canada must be in a very bad way. As a matter of fact, however, the hon. member for Lake Centre displays the same degree of intensity in the presentation of any case he makes to the house. If hon. members will think back over the last three years, they will realize that on occasion, at least by implication, we have found him suggesting apparently that all men of military age should be in our armed services; on another occasion that they should be all overseas; on still another occasion, when he thought we might be threatened here at home, that they should all be on * home defence; on another occasion that they should all be on the farm producing foodstuffs; on another occasion that they should be in our industries producing the materials that are needed in the war. Now I have no doubt that the hon. member wras entitled to present the views he held on these subjects.
I should like to hear the dates on which these various nonexistent statements were made.

However, I would say to the hon. member for Lake Centre that it is three years since this parliament came into existence and since the present government was placed in charge of the war effort of this country. During all that time the hon. member for Lake Centre seemed to have nothing but condemnation for the government. He continuously puts forward the suggestion of complete failure on the part of the government in conducting the war effort of this country.
Let us look at the facts in this fourth year of war. The Minister of National Defence has told us that this small country, starting from scratch, has now an army overseas and at home totalling some 440,000 men. In addition, we have heard the Minister of National Defence for Air tell us that we have now in that force a personnel of some 180,000 men. We know also that in the Royal Canadian Navy there are some 55,000 men. In addition, great numbers of aur young women have enlisted and are taking part in our war effort.
Let us view the results that have been obtained during the years the hon. member for Lake Centre has been condemning the war effort put forth by this government. Does he not agree with me that Canada's war effort is magnificent? In the light of the results it cannot be spoken of other than highly. The production of foodstuffs is constantly mounting; and not only do we in this country, but our allies stand amaze'd at our production of armaments, of guns, of shells, of planes, of ships, and of all the accoutrements of war. I suggest to the hon. member for Lake Centre that he view these things with a little more reason and that he try to see some value in the leadership that this government has given to this country during this time of war.
My main purpose in rising was to bring to the attention of the committee something which I think reflects great credit upon the government, and particularly upon the Minister of National Defence. This is something that came to my attention only during the Easter recess. In this connection I must plead a certain amount of neglect in not knowing that such an organization had been set up. Since my return I asked four other members of this house if they knew about this organization, and I found that they also had failed to notice it's existence. I thought I could do justice to the Minister of National Defence and perhaps give some publicity to this most excellent organization by bringing it to the attention of the committee to-day. I refer to the dependents' board of trustees set up by the Department of National Defence.
This board has been in existence since January, 1942. It was created by order in council to operate under the authority of the

War Appropriation-Army
Minister of National Defence. Its headquarters are in Ottawa and it has branch offices throughout the dominion. In my own province of Saskatchewan there is a branch office at Regina and one at Saskatoon. The purpose of the dependents' board of trustees is to provide special assistance to the dependents of men serving in the Canadian navy, army or air force. This assistance may be either financial, over and above what is received already under existing marriage or dependents' allowance regulations, or it may be non-financial in character. The regional committee can offer advice and arrange for assistance to be given in all types of problems through the various organizations in the different communities. Of course, only those who are in receipt of dependents' allowances are entitled to assistance under this particular board.
Application is made direct to the nearest dependents' advisory committee, and eath application is investigated carefully by a qualified person. I may say that I secured my information from Mr. Dunn, formerly of the dependents' allowance board. I seized the opportunity of finding out some of the details of the benefits given by this particular board. I was greatly pleased at the work that is being done throughout Canada. Grants may be allowed to help to meet expenses due to sickness, hospitalization, doctors', dentists' or opticians' bills, X-rays, surgical appliances, et cetera. They are also given for funeral expenses, special educational costs, losses due to calamity, extra living expenses of large families which consist of more than four children, although this particular item is largely made inoperative by the change in the separation allowance provisions. Other cases of unusual financial difficulty may be taken care of at the discretion of the board.
Apparently wide discretion is given to the board. Where the need is certain; where it is known that the income of the dependent is not sufficient to take care of the need, the board is sufficiently equipped with authority and with means to make an investigation and to act quickly. For instance, I was told that should a man in one of our armed services be lying at death's door, let us say in Halifax, and his dependent was in my home city of Swift Current, if she were unable to provide the funds to get to her husband's bedside, these funds would be furnished by the dependents' board of trustees.
How long would that take?

I gathered from Mr. Dunn that it would take only a very brief period of time because the board recognizes that if they are to be of use in such cases, the assistance must be given speedily.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

When the committee rose at six o'clock I was outlining the work of the dependents' board of trustees and the assistance which that board was prepared to give to those in receipt of dependents' allowances. I have only a few more words to say with regard to that particular matter.
The pamphlet which I hold in my hand, and which is issued by the board, makes it clear that grants made by the board are not loans; that they are not repayable, and that they do not affect regular pay and allowance cheques. The board does not offer charity. Its object is to "help dependents in cases of special hardship or emergency.
1 feel, as I said at the opening of my remarks on this particular matter, that the Minister of National Defence and the government are to be given a great deal of credit for thus taking care of a difficult problem in a very practical way. I would suggest to the Minister of National Defence that, since it was apparent to me that a great many hon. members were unaware of the work which was being done by this board, which I understand has spent in the neighbourhood of a million and a quarter dollars on this work, some greater degree of publicity be given to the board. Its work will recommend itself, I believe, to everybody in Canada. Remembering back to my own experience in the army, I am certain that nothing will give greater comfort to those who are serving away from home, on land, on the sea, or in the air, than the knowledge that the ones whom they leave at home are being taken care of in any emergency that may present itself. Those who have had the experience will agree with me that, when it is suggested we are fighting for democracy, or for Canada, it is only in our better moments, when we meditate upon it, that we realize that this is true. It is rather vague and therefore' difficult for the average person to make the thing tangible and real to his own mind. But there is a little portion of a person's world, inhabited either by his mother, his wife, his children, or perhaps his sweetheart, which is very real to him and which accompanies him in the worst moments of battle; and it is a source of very great
War Appropriation-Army

comfort to that soldier, that air force man or that sailor to know that the government and the people of Canada are collectively seeing to it that his dependents are not faced with some emergency while he is away fighting for his country.
Therefore I suggest to the minister in the light of my own experience, and despite the fact that Mr. Dunn, the officer, who displays a great deal of enthusiasm and interest in this particular work, assures me that the board is in every way possible publicizing its existence and the benefits it gives to the dependents, that even that is not sufficient and that further publicity should be given. As Mr. Dunn and I were sitting in a car a soldier happened to sit opposite us, and I tested the publicity which had been given to this matter in the army by asking him if he knew of the provisions of the particular order in council setting up this board of trustees. First, he said he did not, and then, as I recalled some of the benefits, he said, "Yes, I recall now that it was posted on the order board." But unfortunately soldiers are usually busy; when they are not busy they are probably in a hurry to get somewhere else. The result was, the soldier readily confessed that he failed to read carefully the particular publication which gave his unit the notice on the order board. So that I suggest to the minister, knowing soldiers, that probably it would be wise to have the officers of each unit, during a lecture on discipline, if you will, or on some other suitable occasion, read and point out the advantages of this particular measure, and that the soldiers be invited in turn to send word to their dependents.
I find that there is considerable knowledge regarding this particular board in the centres where the district offices are. But Canada remains largely a rural country made up of farms, villages and towns; and I suggest to the minister that he use the weekly newspapers to give further publicity to the advantages of this particular board.
May I ask the hon. member, merely for information, whether he knows how many officers are established to-day in Saskatchewan and how many grants have been made. Has he that information?

I have not that information with me. There is one point raised by the hon. member for Weyburn which I should like to emphasize to the minister, namely, that the investigation be speedy, though necessari'y thorough, and that the relief be given as quickly as humanly possible under the circumstances.
May I say to the committee-and to the public, if my voice reaches that far-that a necessary corollary is that those of us who have the opportunity, in the communities in which we live and where dependents are entitled to the benefits of this measure, should try to see to it that the type of persons we denominate as chisellers are kept out of the picture. As I look back over the previous war and its aftermath, the pension acts which were in force, and, in the interval, the relief acts and other measures of that kind, it is clear that the person who deliberately, on false pretences, secures a measure of assistance to which he is not entitled, is the person who creates the necessity for rigid regulations and a slow process of securing the benefits of these remedial acts, and causes a great many of our difficulties. I think the time has come in Canada when, before embarking on any programme of enlightened social service, we should try to educate our communities and our people to recognize that they are partners with government in the giving of these benefits, and that "chisellers" are only taking from those who deserve that measure of benefit and that easy access to benefits to which they are entitled under the act.
There is another matter I should like to draw to the attention of the minister. In speaking to an officer-a veteran, by the "way, of the Dieppe affair-who recently returned from England, I naturally took the opportunity of asking about our troops overseas. He reported that in his opinion the morale was very high indeed. But in our discussion he made it clear to me that he was concerned about a matter, which the minister himself has mentioned on more than one occasion in this chamber, namely, the sending to men overseas, by relatives or friends, perhaps with good intent, letters stating that something terrible has happened to a loved one at home. This officer, who was a company commander, told me that he has noticed excellent men in his particular company for whom, on receipt of that type of news from home, the whole world seemed to have collapsed and who lost that spirit of high morale which every soldier should have and to which he is entitled in the environment he is in. The minister has called our attention to this, but I wish to pass on to him the suggestion this particular officer made. He thought it was sufficiently important for the morale of the troops overseas that some arrangement be made whereby officers commanding the different units would have authority to cable to a central office in Canada, which office through the different war services could collect the correct information

War Appropriation-Army
with regard to the particular case, and send it back by cable, so that if the news were untrue an authoritative denial could be given to the soldier, and if unfortunately there was some measure of truth in the news imparted by the relative, it could be broken to the soldier in the proper way and as much salvaged from the domestic trouble as possible. I pass that on, because I was much impressed with the emphasis which the officer, so lately home from England, placed on that particular point.
The last matter I wish to deal with before I sit down is one which fortunately is receiving, I understand, exhaustive inquiry, and that, by a body of men authorized by the government and including not only members of the armed services but men in civilian life; I refer to the use of our medical men in the armed services, having in mind also the need for them among the civilian population. I am given to understand that there are approximately eleven thousand graduates of medical schools in Canada. Some three thousand of these are in the armed services. In Canada- and I speak only of Canada-there are approximately 1,400 in the army, 576 in the air force and 270 in the navy. The Royal Canadian Army Medical Corps, in addition to its usual work, takes care of prisoners of war, the allied units training in Canada, a great deal of work in connection with army hospitals, and, I assume, other duties which I have not noted. My point in raising this matter is that the minister, when the report of the committee which is making an exhaustive and overall survey of the use of medical men, both in the army and out of it, in Canada to-day, and which report is, I think, coming down fairly soon, is submitted, he have the benefit of at least my opinion with regard to the subject.
My own attitude has been determined largely by my experience in the last war, by many conversations I have had fairly recently with army medical officers and with civilian medical men, and, in addition, by the information which I gained on the war expenditures committee. I am sometimes of the opinion that, with regard to the use of our medical men, we are still back in the days of the Boer war. I am informed that prior to that time medical men were not attached to units as such; they were not on the establishment of the unit. They did not have in those days the standing which they have now and which they properly deserve, but for a long period it has been the custom, as we all know, to attach a medical officer to a unit. The battalion has its medical officer and he is on the establishment of that particular unit. We
all know that men who are enlisted are in a very healthy state; fortunately their ills, other than injuries, are not usually many or serious; and the work of the average medical officer in a battalion is comparatively light. It seems to me, therefore, that we are not recognizing the immense step-up in transportation, in the facility of getting medical men to a given group-I am speaking only of Canada and not of conditions overseas-and we should recognize this fact and make more economical use of our medical men in the armed forces.
In discussing the matter with the director general of medical services to-day, I am happy to say that the committee is aware of almost every thought that I had on the subject and is giving it consideration. I have no doubt the report will deal with these matters. My belief is that we would be wiser to adopt the method of not attaching medical officers to any given unit but rather of keeping them in a pool so that they could be used for any group that might require medical assistance. With modern methods of transportation that assistance could be placed very quickly at the disposal of men anywhere and would save man-power, and, in addition, large sums of money, and would give to the men in the service even better medical attention than they now receive.
I have also in mind the fact that there is a shortage in many districts in Canada, and I suggest that we should make the best use of the man-power in the medical sendees for our army and our medical needs. The two of them must be considered together. I feel, too, that there is a wastage, and I say this after my own experience in the last war, if it is paralleled by the experience gained in this. There is a wastage in the capabilities of the doctor himself. It is trying for an expert not to use his expert knowledge over any long period, and there is an inclination for the doctor who has very few duties to vegetate and to lose that capacity which this nation will need not only now but in the post-war period.
I suggest to the minister, therefore, that when the report of the committee is presented to him he should not regard it in the light of conditions as they now exist either here or in the United States or in the mother country, because, as in all things in this war, the use of our medical men should be viewed from the year 1943 and the knowledge we now have, and the very best possible use made of our manpower resources in that particular regard.
There is nothing else I wish to say. I have already stated that the committee is examining into all these matters and I anticipate with
War Appropriation-Army

great interest the submission of that report. I trust that our whole position will be studied carefully by the government and particularly by the Minister of National Defence.

What I shall have to say in regard to any military matters will deal purely with questions of policy. I sympathize with the minister in the lack of interest shown by this committee and by the public in the war. I also sympathize with the minister in the fact that he had to put his long and complicated statement on the record in dribs and drabs, fifteen minutes here, ten minutes there. I know that nothing is more difficult than to put a long and complicated statement on the record over a period of several days.
The condition in which we find ourselves and a lack of fighting fnterest in the war can be blamed on the policy of the government in easing the country carefully and slowly into total wftr. I know I shall be met with the criticism, what about the victory loan? True, the objective was reached; in fact a greater sum was raised. But it was raised, despite the increased number of individual buyers, very largely by floating capital and financial institutions. Invested savings accounts are still to a degree intact in our financial institutions. I think that is a symptom of the lack of real warlike spirit evident in the country to-day, and, as I say, the minister has my sympathy.
A good deal has been said in this committee about Dieppe. I will confine my remarks to matters of policy concerning this operation. There was a certain amount of surprise felt by the minister and others in the fact that the Germans were in a state of preparedness, awareness, and had recently reinforced their coastal area. That, in my opinion, is due very largely to our policy of advertising. On July 16. 1912, the London Times carried this item, and the Daily Telegraph practically devoted its whole front page to Canadian manoeuvres on the southeast coast. The Times headline reads:
Biggest invasion manoeuvres. Canadians, Navy and It.A.F. in action.
It goes on to say:
The biggest raid and invasion manoeuvres ever held in European waters have just been completed by a powerful Canadian force working in conjunction with the Royal Navy and the RAF. A Canadian war correspondent describes it as "a prelude to what may be major military operations on the European coast."
It went on to say that several naval craft put out to sea and mentioned that General McNaughton, General Crerar and Lord Mount-batten watched.
A description of the craft engaged in the manoeuvres was given. It is very easy to see
[Mr. Graham.1
what happened from the giving out of this information. It was obvious to the Germans that we were planning some type of raid. They [DOT] must have known it through the German embassy in Dublin. The English newspapers pass freely to Dublin, where they are no doubt read in minute detail by members of the German embassy staff. We had given them fair warning that there was a raid coming off. That was on July 16. Dieppe took place on August 19. The Germans know, as we know, that an amphibian raid upon a coast can be carried out only at certain phases of the tide, in certain types of weather, with a certain amount of cloud cover and favourable direction of wind. They know that just as well as we do. Therefore the German, being a reasonable animal, must have been extremely alert over that period when tide, moon and weather were favourable to,a raid. I think such a policy of giving out information about manoeuvres, particularly large manoeuvres on that scale, is a faulty policy; I think it is the wrong policy.
There was at that time another army in England) also carrying out training in amphibian attacks, an army which -was also preparing for a landing. That army was the first army. Yet nothing at all was said in the press about the training of that army. That was the right policy. The other policy was, I think, in error. I believe it had much to do with the awareness of the Germans, and their great concentration of forces all up and1 down that coast. We hacl given them fair warning. I think that is a just criticism.
The success of any commando raid-j. shall not go into detail-is judged by the speed with which the raiding force gets off the beach. There has recently been published a book entitled, "Combined Operations", an official document published by his majesty's stationery office, giving the official description of the Dieppe raid. I would strongly recommend it as reading to all members of the house. From it they will be a"ble to judge the speed at which the raiding force was able to get off the beach.
There is one other item with regard to the Dieppe operation upon which I wish to touch, namely, the time of the raid. It was a daylight or early morning raid. "Combined Operations" say that the raid took place in daylight. The timing is a question of policy. The experience of the Russians in repelling the Germans on prev'ious occasions, particularly on one of the islands in the gulf of Finland, was that a daylight or early morning raid did not give the chances of success that complete darkness did.
Before leaving the subject of Dieppe I should like to quote the last four lines in "Combined

War Appropriation-Army
Operations", which is the official document on the operation. These are the lines, at page 140:
By now-
It is speaking of the second attempt to reinforce.
-it was obvious that the headlands to the east and west of Dieppe could not be captured in time to permit an entry into the town; the doors were, in fact, still closed. It was decided to withdraw those who had been assaulting them and the town so intrepidly.
This chapter in the book should, I believe, be read by all hon. members. It is official, and gives one of the most interesting descriptions of combined operations. That is all I mean to say on the Dieppe operation.
This afternoon in this house a most extraordinary suggestion, was put forward. The suggestion was made that the draftees, now given the opprobrium of "zombies", should be sent to Alaska to relieve the United States garrison there which would then be free to fight in combat service. If that suggestion should be adopted there would be more Canadian casualties ip the bar rooms of the world than we ever suffered in war. No Canadian would dare show his face anywhere outside Canada; we would be the laughingstock of the world. If Clare Luce, Colonel McCormick and those other wild people in the United States ever hear of this suggestion, we shall have a lot of explaining to do. Our reputation will be as low as that of the Portuguese after the last war. To suggest that we allow somebody else, another nation, to do our fighting for us is the most fantastic thing ever to have been said in this house, and I wish to protest as vigorously as I possibly can against that suggestion, which I think is simply appalling.
We have mentioned the question of manpower. I want to deal with that matter, looking at the situation as it at present exists. The danger of an invasion of Canada is becoming more and more remote. I was never one of those who thought we were in serious danger of invasion, but perhaps that was because I come from the central part of Canada. I listened to expressions from east and west and said nothing, because I thought the people on the spot should know the situation best. Now, however, with the attack on the Aleutian islands; with Attu virtually fallen and Kiska probably coming next; with the invasion of the continent of Europe imminent, I believe the danger of an invasion of Canada by a land force must be regarded as extremely remote. We have troops earmarked for that contingency. I believe one of our first duties should be to
evaluate the situation and see what can be done to make these troops available for combat service overseas. I do not know what percentage of the sixth, seventh and eighth divisions are home defence personnel, but I submit that the keeping of these three divisions as a potential against invasion is an unsound use of mam-.power.
These are some of the matters with which I think the government should deal at a secret session, when the minister could give us a free and frank evaluation of the possibilities of invasion. He is in possession of reports and information not available to others; but to the lay mind it does seem that there is very little possibility of these troops being used in any operational role in Canada.
The coastal garrisons offer another source of man-power. Naturally we cannot be told where the garrisons are, or their size, but the troops making up these garrisons are not as likely to be called upon to defend our coasts now as they were last year or the year before, and I believe at a secret session we should have a frank statement of . the possibility of releasing some of these operational troops for combat duty overseas. The minister spoke about a home war establishment of eighty thousand. We should be able to reduce that establishment. He spoke about forty members of the training staff, headquarters staff and so on being required to train one hundred recruits. Despite the fact that this appears to be a large number, I think it is quite reasonable. The training establishment in Canada has been well and efficiently conducted. The job of training men for the army is being efficiently carried on, and I am quite convinced that the training given in Canada during the four months' period is equal to the training given in a similar period of time anywhere else in the world; in fact I believe in most instances the Canadian training is superior. The training centres are well run and well managed. and they are doing a fine job of training our men. I believe that from now until the end of the war the role of the army in Canada will be purely that of training, and that operational troops will not have a necessary function to fulfil.
We have spoken of the fact that we have raised 750.000 in all services, army, navy and air force, with a population of eleven and a half or eleven and three-quarters million. I do not wish to make unnecessary comparisons; but before we take unto ourselves too much credit for having raised this many men, let us look for a moment at what Australia has done, a country with a little over six million people.
War Appropriation-Army

The official news letter from Australia contains a statement by Prime Minister Curtin to the effect that in the past three months the men sworn into the fighting services had risen from 750,000 to 800,000. That is from a country of slightly over six million people. The Australian imperial force, the Royal Australian Air Force and the Royal Australian Navy has increased in three months from
422,000	to 500,000. Those are overseas troops. This news letter contains the further information that more than one man in three, of those between the ages of eighteen and forty, had joined the overseas armed forces.
The criticism will be made that Australia is not as great a manufacturing or industrial country. But Australian factory workers in essential war jobs number 539,000, or seventy per cent of the nation's total factory employees. That is a very, very magnificent effort. Before we talk about our having reached our largest possible army, or our saturation point in respect of man-power, we should look at the Australian figures, and see what is happening in that commonwealth. I shall not mention New Zealand, where the figures are even better.
It is apparent that in our industrial war effort we have reached a climacteric, and that we are changing over from smaller weapons to larger ones. I gather from the press that we have ceased the manufacture of tanks. We have reached the stage where the gun is beating the armour. That will require a very great dislocation of industry.
I am fearful, not of a lack of man-power to fulfil the job; I am more fearful of unemployment than anything else. It takes time, trouble and industry to retool factories. How many of them will have to be retooled, and what the changes will be, I do not know. But we are warned that they will be very considerable. Let us beware that we do not find ourselves with a period, temporary if you like, of unemployment.
There has been a suggestion that the Canadian army should be broken up, that our army overseas should be split and merged -with other parts of the British army. I hope that is not government policy. I hope it is not the policy of this government to split up the army. It is easy to sit comfortably here and suggest that the Canadian army has not done any fighting. It is also easy to adv.ocate sending somebody else into battle. The only reason for advocating battle training is that when the Canadian army does attack the fortress of Germany it wil 1 have fewer casualties.
The one basic reason for training is to be able to kill the enemy before he kills you.
fMr. Adamson.]
That is why the well-trained army suffers fewer casualties than the army which has not had those training advantages. I submit it was a mistake not to have allowed some of the Canadian units to see service in Africa. Whether it was offered or not, I am not in a position to say. But had we had a brigade, or even a division of troops in Africa-

The hon. member has said it was a mistake not to permit Canadians to be used in Africa. There is the suggestion in that remark that someone refused permission,
Mr, ADAMSON: I never said that permission was refused.

My hon. friend's expression was that it was a mistake not to permit them. May I say to him there was no suggestion of not permitting them. I have made it clear to the committee that there has been the freest opportunity for suggestions to us to make any use which, could be made of the Canadian army, either in units or as a whole. North Africa was one of them. But there was no suggestion that they would not be permitted, to go there, if it had been so desired or suggested.

I should not have used
the word "permit." Rather I should have referred to an opportunity. I believe that had a brigade or a division had experience in Africa, it would have been in better position now to undertake the very serious job of attacking the continent of Europe. When this attack will come, how it will come or where it will come is known only to the high command. But that we shall take part in it is obvious.
Despite what the minister has said, I hope the Canadians will act as an army. I do not know any reason for splitting them up, but there have been reports in the press to the effect that there are possibilities of splitting the Canadian forces. In my opinion that would be a mistake.
There are two jobs to-day, one in Europe and the other in the orient. It is unthinkable that we should consider that our responsibilities are confined only to the continent of Europe. We are a Pacific power just as much as we are an Atlantic power. Our responsibilities in the Pacific are just as great as they are in the Atlantic. We must consider that we have an enemy in the Pacific as well as an enemy in Europe. We must be prepared to attack the enemy in the Pacific as well as in Europe. We must be prepared, as all the members of the united nations must be prepared, in the words of Mr. Churchill, to come

War Appropriation-Army
to grips with the enemy on the largest possible scale in the shortest possible time. That is our problem; that is our responsibility.
To have a large army which can see service only in Canada will become more and more difficult for our national pride to bear. As the tide of war turns, certainly after a bridgehead has been established, we shall be the subject of ridicule for keeping a home-defence-only army in Canada. If it is,the stated policy of the government not to send the home defence personnel out of Canada under any circumstances, then that fact should-be stated and stated fairly soon. If it is the policy of the government to send home defence personnel out of Canada, in fairness to the men themselves they should be told what is expected of them. I submit that the whole question of man-power hangs on this one thing, the home defence army. Are we prepared to face our responsibilities as every other member of the united nations has faced them and be ready to seek out and destroy the enemy where we can, or are we to play the role of keeping back large forces in Canada-[DOT]

Surely my hon. friend
knows there is a limitation on sending troops out of Australia? He knows there is no conscription of any kind in South Africa. What does my hon. friend mean by saying that all the other nations send their troops out of the country?
Australia is in imminent danger, or was up to a short time ago and probably is still.
And her conscription act permits her to send troops only as far north as the equator.
She was in imminent danger of land invasion.
I do not see that that is justification for my hon. friend to say that other allied nations have the right to send their troops anywhere.

Australia was definitely in a war zone. Australian troops have suffered casualties while on Australia territory. Australia is in a war zone; we are not. That is the difference between the Australian system and ours. That is the point I was trying to make. The South African system is, of course, different.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Does my hon. friend know that the system in Australia is the same as the system here, perhaps not quite as strict?

I was explaining to the Minister of National Defence that Australia had been subjected to physical enemy attack. Apart from a few shells fired from a submarine, our country has not been subjected to attack and it is unlikely that we shall be. The war is receding from Canada; the war is not receding from Australia.
Therefore?
Therefore I contend that to compare our system with that of Australia is not a tenable argument.

I am not arguing; I am just correcting my hon. friend on the facts. My hon. friend stated, or at least I understood him to state, that other allied nations had the right to send their troops anywhere. I am pointing out that that is not true in Australia or South Africa.
The case in South Africa is probably similar to ours, but the combat zone is receding from South Africa.
South Africa has no conscription. They had to pass an act to allow them to send volunteers out of the country.
The South African situation is one that we would hardly like to-
I am simply stating a fact and I think my hon. friend might accept the fact.
I will accept the fact about South Africa.
And about Australia?

The difference between us and Australia is the fact that Australia is in a combat area and we are not. I grant to the minister that Australia, has limitations on the sending of men outside the country north of the equator, but the situation is not the same because Australia is definitely in a combat zone, and troops called up for service inside Australia have become casualties and have been subject to enemy attack. There was a time, at Port Darwin particularly, when an enemy landing on Australian soil was considered quite probable. I think the situation in Australia is different.
Compared with Canada, that country is sixty per cent the size, but it has raised 500,000 men for overseas service, and has in its armed forces a total of 800,000 men. Actually the force they have raised is much larger than what we have raised.

Where does my hon. friend get those figures?

This is an extract from the Australian imperial force and the Royal Australian Air Force news letter for the week ended April 29, 1943. The document comes to me with the compliments of the high commissioner for the commonwealth of Australia. Does that satisfy the minister?
I have some figures here which were given me in confidence.
I am sorry the minister's figures are not up to date. I shall be glad to give him these when I have finished with them.
These figures were given to me in confidence; I did not know they had been published.
I heard them over the air.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have to inform the hon. member that he has spoken for over forty minutes.
May I just finish my statement? I was interrupted considerably.
No.
Be fair. The hon. member was interrupted.
Go ahead.

All I was going to say was that this is the whole crux of our manpower problem: either these men should be told to be prepared to fight anywhere, or, as the war recedes, some other use should be made of them.

When we discuss estimates we must come down to some elementary facts, and there must be some admissions of certain elementary truths which serve as the basis for a discussion. Since I see the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton in his seat, may I tell him I regret what I said the other day, on account of the courageous stand he took on behalf of the farmers of his county last year. I want to give everyone his due, and sometimes in the heat of discussion words are said which are more or less regrettable. The hon. member has well defended the farmers of his county and of the east, as also has the hon. member for Lambton-Kent; I give them credit for that.
At six o'clock we were discussing agriculture. The hon. member for Swift Current said a few words about it; and I was following the hon. member for Lake Centre, and speaking of the question which was put at the time of the plebiscite and the meaning of it. What astounded me is that after the plebiscite was over, anyone could have thought that the
majority which voted "yes" was for an altogether different question from that which was put to the people. I have not the exact terms of that question, but it was to this effect: Are you in favour of relieving the government of the pledge that has been given to the Canadian people, and so on: yes or no. The question, Are you for conscription for overseas or not? has not been put by any minister. Just before six o'clock, according to the notes I have taken, the Minister of National Defence admitted that he had not put the question, and he added the second time, " I did not frame the question for the plebiscite and had nothing to do with the passing of the orders in council except as a member of the government." And then he said, " I have put the [DOT] question as the question was framed." That was clear. I did not accuse him of having drafted the question. But there is ministerial solidarity, and as a member of the cabinet he was just as responsible as anjr other minister for the drafting of these questions, whether they were penned in his own hand or that of one of his colleagues; that is immaterial. But what I say is that the question which was put to the Canadian people was not one which justified conscription for service overseas, and many hon. members representing constituencies outside Quebec have told me after the plebiscite that there was at the time no question whatever of conscription for service overseas.
There is another question that is very important. It is the corollary of the basis of the discussion, namely, that agriculture is an essential industry in times of war as well as in times of peace. That is fundamental, and I am not afraid to say so in view of the numerous speeches from all corners of the house in defence of the farmer. And that defence has been made quite eloquently by a number of men of imperialist feelings. But, here is the corollary to the first statement. It is that the farmer has not been given the same glory, the same glamour as the man in the army-and of course they are different occupations. But my contention, considering the numerous speeches that have been made by a large number of hon. members, is that the farmer is just as necessary and just as honourable as the soldier. The soldier has been eulogized at the expense of the farmer. Mind you, it is often much more pleasing for a boy who comes from the country to be in one of the branches of the army than to be on the farm, and- if he stays on the farm it is because he has a family duty to perform in helping his aged or sick father to run the farm. I know manv hovs who have enlisted
War Appropriation-Army

and are content to be in the army, and others who would like to join but cannot do so because they are obliged to stay at home to do some important work on the farm. They cannot leave, and when they do not join the army they are at times regarded as slackers, men who do not do their duty.
This was the feeling of the ex-chairman of the Quebec board. That is the way he thought and the way he spoke on many occasions. He considered all the young ablebodied farmers who stayed on the farm as slackers, unworthy of Canadian citizenship. The orders in council of March last, regarding selective service, were simply an inducement to the farmer to vote "yes" to that senseless question that was then put to the people of Canada. Some farmers were fooled by it, and afterwards it was said that they had been in favour of conscription for service overseas. The stand I take is that if the army is to be maintained, one thing is essential, namely, that it should be provided with proper food and clothing, and the army can get this only from the farms. Therefore the work of the farmer is essentia], both to the army and to the civilian population. That is my point, and I cannot understand why the farmer receives from the army treatment different from that which he receives from the Department of Labour.
The other day I asked a question about a phoenix of the Department of National Defence, a brass hat. I am told by some people who have been to his office that he is very bold and lacks manners entirely. Here is the question:
1.	Is Captain K. D. Andrews employed in the Department of National Defence at Ottawa?
2.	If so, (a) since when; (b) in what position; (c) what is his age?
3.	What is his military record?
4.	What experience has he had as an agriculturist, where, and for what period?
5.	Are there other agricultural experts employed in the Department of National Defence?
6.	If so. (a) what are their ages; (b) what is their military record; (c) what agricultural experience have they had?
1.	Yes
2.	(a) 8th December, 1941.
(b) Staff captain.
(e) 47 years.
3.	Jamaica Militia Artillery 1913-15. British West India Regiment 1916-19. Royal Regiment of Canada since August, 1940. Saw active service during 1914-18 in Egypt, Belgium, France and Italy.
4.	None, so far as is known.
5.	No personnel are employed for the purpose of serving as agricultural experts.
6.	Answered by 5 above.
Here is a man in the adjutant-general's branch who knows nothing about agriculture. He has no experience. They have no experts
fMr. Pnuliot.l
in agriculture in the Department of National Defence, and yet they decide whether a farmer who is in the army should stay in the army or go back to the farm. They know nothing about it. I have the admission of the minister, and all hon. members have the faculty of seeing that. The return is dated May 6, but I do not know whether it was tabled that day. According to what was said by the minister, there is not a single agricultural expert in the Department of National Defence, and they are the people who pass judgment upon the usefulness of a man on the farm or in the army. There is a password, "Get as many men as you can, whether they are sick or well. Get the men and keep them there." If I started to discuss those who are sick and are kept there doing nothing, paid by the government, and in hospital, I would have a long story to tell. But I can give numbers that cannot be denied. I will not give names, but I can give numbers, and every file from which I have obtained information is at the disposal of the-minister. For six months each year I have been listening to complaints of soldiers. I have received them by hundreds, complaining of the way in which they have been dealt with by these men who pass on their record. Did this man really have that military record? He went through the world to fight in the last war. but-
What is that statement?

He went through the world, Egypt, Jamaica, everywhere, but he did not see any farm; he did not work on a farm; that is the only thing he did not do; and he is deciding on farmers in a very bold way. I know the minister will defend him. He is like a hen that has been sitting on ducks' eggs.
I suggest that this gentleman has about as much ability to decide on farmers as my hon. friend has to decide about soldiers.	[DOT]

I will inform the minister about what is going on in his department and I will tell him the truth. I will not flatter him, and when 1 am through with him he will be finished. Let us ask him another question. How many condoms did he requisition from the department of health? Will he tell me the number of condoms he purchased from the Department of Pensions and National Health? I want his answer. Is it true that once-
Will my hon. friend-

Sit down, please. I have not finished my question.
