Mr. Chairman, this wild man has asked me a question.

Mr. Chairman, I want
him to withdraw that word. He has no reason for calling me "wild" when I use mild language.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Temiscouata was asking a question of the minister, and surely the minister should have an opportunity to reply.
My hon. friend has asked me three questions already. There is an item coming up in the estimates in connection with medical supplies, and I will answer my hon. friend's question then.

That is all right. Let the minister use his pencil and take notes. He will have to take many notes. We will ask about condoms wrapped1 in fake Nouvelles Catholiques-English condoms wrapped in French, in fake Nouvelles Catholiques to hide them.
But let us proceed with the farm worker. I have a few papers in front of me, Mr. Chairman. I have much more to say about medical supplies, but I will leave that for the moment. I shall also have a word to say about a brigadier who was degraded. He was the one who had kept a member of parliament for forty-two days in gaol.
I want now to give the case-and I am not wild; I am quiet-of a young man, Roland Pinette, aged sixteen, who enlisted without the consent of his father. I wrote in April to have him sent home. No definite answer has yet been given. I hope the minister will look into this matter. This young man was born on September 7, 1926. I wonder if he will be kept in the army until he is seventeen and if they will then say: It is too late.
Is my hon. friend handing me the file?
Oh, yes. This young man is at Rimouski.

What is my hon. friend doing? Is he going to give the particulars? I cannot do anything if there is just a reference to somebody who enlisted when he was just sixteen unless his name and number are given.

That is all right; I will satisfy the minister. I have the particulars under my hand. The name of this young man is Roland Pinette, fils d'Honore, of St. Eusebe (Riviere Cabano), Temiscouata
county. His birth certificate was sent to the officer commanding at Rimouski, and the minister's department has been notified.
Did he enlist, or was he called up?

He may have enlisted, but without the consent of his parents. He was only sixteen.
There is another thing I cannot understand. There was a dispatch in the Evening Citizen of March 24, 1943, headed "To retain only men with A categories". The item is as fallows:
Calgary, March 23-Men called up for military service under the National Resources Mobilization Act, who receive a medical category lower than A1 or A2, will not be inducted into the service but will be allowed to return home, it was stated in new instructions received to-day by the Calgary board.
In a few cases men who are graded as B1 will be retained if they follow a special trade.
In the past, all men who received a category of B2 or higher were retained in the service.
I have received many letters from parents of soldiers who needed their sons at home. They would write me and say: My son is in category B or category C, and I want him at home. They had seen in the papers this item of news from Calgary. It has been published in all the Ontario and Quebec papers, and in view of that item in the press I cannot understand why the army keeps these young men who are in B or C category'.

If these men are in the army and are in category Bl, B2 or C, they are kept in the army because there are certain places where men in those categories can be used. The reason for the rule to which my hon. friend referred a moment ago whereby men below category A1 or A2 were not being accepted was that we did not want to get the service filled with low category men. It may be that we shall have an opportunity to take in more men. We are not releasing those who are already in, but we are not taking in any more of them except for special jobs.

I thank the minister for his answer. It is much better for him to proceed in that way than to call me "wild". He will get much farther by answering me in that way than he will by calling me names. Howevqr, the minister must understand the confusion in the minds of the parents after reading that item. Certainly they have been greatly embarrassed. But if the army needs mostly category A and A1 men I do not see when an application is made to release a farmer's son in B or lower category, why it should be refused.

The answer is that if we let him go we will have to fill his place with a category A man.

I thank the minister for his answer, but I doubt that he is right, because it is very easy for the army to get other men who are in categories lower than A and who are ready to enlist. I am sure that if the minister has listened to the speeches which have been made about man-power requirements in agriculture, he will agree that agriculture is just as essential as the army and that it would be unfair to keep in the army as secondary help men who would be of primary help in agriculture. The minister knows very well that a man who has only one eye but who is able-bodied may make an excellent farmer, although he would not be put in categoiy A in the army.
He will very often make an excellent soldier, too.

Yes; he may make an excellent soldier, but I know of young men who have been rejected because they had only one eye. Here we see the viewpoint of the minister. I submit that such a young man may be a good farmer; the minister may agree, but in order to keep that young man in the army he says at once, "Oh, he will make an excellent soldier." I know of young men who have been put in category E because they had only one eye, and that is fair. If they have to use a rifle they need their eyes badly; unless they put the rifle to the wrong shoulder-
It depends upon which eye a man has lost.

The right eye is badly needed. Then let me tell the minister something else, in all kindness. If the Department of National Defence keeps on in this way, it will completely destroy agriculture in this country; it will be the cause of a famine, unless it admits that agriculture is just as important as the army, not only for the sake of the army but for the sake of the civilian population as well. That is simple language, but I will tell him something more. I have been informed that the reason why the Conservative party as a whole-I do not mean the individual members, who are very fine fellows-has not come to the defence of agriculture is that the party is afraid that, if it should do so, the government would at once press for service overseas. I do not say that is true, but T do say that such matters as agriculture never should be used as political footballs. Let me tell the minister, hon. members on this side and hon. members on the other side, that the best way to get and keep the confidence of the people

is not by trying to play politics but to do what one thinks is right, without any thought in mind of power or personal advantage or future ambition. I would ask hon. gentlemen to do as I do, to consider their own constituents before anyone else; then they will have the satisfaction of having done their duty.
I now come back to the farmers. Here is the case of another young man who is in the army; he is No. D-611207, at Valcartier. I have a letter from his father making his third request for the release of this boy from the army. He says that since his son has gone he has had to neglect his farm, because he is alone and cannot do the heavy work. His farm consists of 275 acres, with twenty-seven milch cows, four young calves, three horses, seventy-five hens and a sugar bush with 800 trees. His only help is a young man in feeble health, who delivers the milk; the other children are going to school to complete their studies. He says that his son would be of great help to him and could do his war effort in producing food for the allies. That gentleman lives at Magog, in Stanstead county, which seat is vacant just now.
How long has the man been in the army?
This letter is dated April 6, but it is the third request.

Was he called up, or did
he enlist?

I do not know; I think he
was called up. .
Then he would have an opportunity to apply to the board for postponement.
No; he must apply to his officer commanding.
When he was called up he would have the right to apply to the board.
Yes, but the board said, "Go to the army."
Then it was not the army who said that; it was the board.
Yes, on the requisition of the minister for more men.

The hon. gentleman will remember that the board is not composed of army men. It is headed by a judge and composed of people who are in no way connected with the army, and there is an agricultural representative in attendance. That board must have refused the application of that young man; it must have decided that he was not essential to agriculture. Why put the blame on the army?	.

War Appropriation-Army

I may tell the minister that the representative of agriculture on the Quebec board is a lumber scaler who has been appointed by the minister for air, who lives at St. Pacome and who has not even a garden. The only satisfaction I have obtained for farmers has been from the representative of the selective service, who is a Quebec manufacturer.
How does he know anything about farming?

He has common sense,
which is a good thing to have. There is a letter on file from the secretary-treasurer of the town of Magog, certifying that he has known this young man for several years; that the young man has worked on his father's farm, and that his father delivers about 150 quarts of milk daily in the town of Magog. The father is described in this letter as a model farmer, and this gentleman recommends that the son be given leave of absence from the army for the summer and fall months so that he may return to his previous occupation. That letter, as well as the letter from the father, is sworn before a notary public. There is a sworn statement also from the official agronomist to the same effect, who mentions the 800 maple trees and says that this man is a good farmer. There is also a letter from the parish priest, sworn before a notary.
I have much more to say about the farmers, but first I have something else to tell the minister. He knows about farming, of course; on his registration card in 1940 he stated that lie had milked a cow for three months in the maritimes. Perhaps that was not the. only time he milked a cow, but that was something, so that he cannot say that he has totally ignored the problems of agriculture.
There are other cases. I have in mind particularly blacksmiths' helpers, who are most necessary to the farmers. They must be available all year round, not only to shoe horses, but also to repair sleighs, carriages, wagons, express trucks and agricultural implements. At the time of mobilization it was well understood that blacksmiths' helpers were badly needed in rural communities. Petitions were signed by mayors, councillors and leading farmers in several communities, asking for postponement of training of certain farmers and blacksmiths.
But the blacksmith is not alone. We could also mention the tinsmith. We do not find a tinsmith in every parish or township. Petitions were signed and resolutions passed by municipal councils and leading people in rural communities asking that blacksmiths be given
postponements, in order to help farmers. Then, what about saddlers, shoemakers and masons? We know it is necessary to have masons within certain areas, so that they may be available to build and repair chimneys, foundations and the like. No one is self-supporting. The agricultural class need help, just the same as the army.
What was the trouble at Dieppe? It was that the auxiliary services were destroyed, and that was the most lamentable part of the battle, with the exception of the loss of life. From the military point of view the destruction of a large part of those auxiliary services was one of the great handicaps suffered by the Canadian army.
We may have in mind a man who has spent his time in building houses or barns for farmers. Perhaps those barns have been destroyed by fire, or in some other way. Such- a man may have to report to his commanding officer. I will tell the minister how that works out in the province of Quebec. When hon. members from other provinces learn how people in Quebec are dealt with, not only by the brass hats here in Ottawa, but by certain French Canadians in charge of regiments, they will have greater sympathy for us than the hon. member for York West may have for the Minister of National Defence-and it will be more sincere.
The young man working on the farm who is called to the army must pass his medical examination, something about which I shall have much to say. May I tell hon, members it is not always pleasant to make observations like that, but I am in- duty bound to do so. And when I have finished my storv it will be just as useful in other constituencies as it is in mine. But that is not the reason why I do it; I do it because it is my duty.
A young farmer may be called by the registrar to attend for medical examination. This happens, after he has heard over the radio and read in the press that farmers' sons are exempted, and are to be treated leniently. He reports to the board and, thanks to the fairness of the present chairman, and certain officials of the national selective service, he may sometimes receive a favourable answer. But if we refer to page 2920 of Hansard for May 21, 1943, we shall find, to the astonishment of the minister himself, and all hon. members, that the city of Quebec has the second smallest percentage of postponements granted. The smallest percentage is credited to Regina, with 61 per cent; Quebec, second, with 70 per cent. London, Ontario, has 93 per cent, or 23 per cent more than the city of Quebec.

' Mr. RALSTON: Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, I think we ought to keep reasonably close to the subject at hand, namely the estimates of the army. The postponements to which my hon. friend is referring have nothing whatsoever to do with the army. They are postponements made by a board appointed under the Department of Labour, and carrying out selective service regulations.
I should imagine the hon. member has almost finished his forty minutes, and I shall make a suggestion to the committee. A statement was made some time ago by me, in the presence of all hon. members in the committee, with no dissenting voice, with regard to a suggestion which had been made as to the way in which the estimates of the various war departments should be dealt with, in order that they might be handled expeditiously and in an orderly fashion.
That suggestion was that each minister should make a statement, and that when the estimates should be discussed, along the same lines as we conduct discussions in respect of ordinary civil estimates. A break-down was given for the army, the navy and the air force, in respect of various items. Since last Tuesday night I have been waiting to enter upon a discussion of those estimates. I realize that hon. members would wish to have a certain amount of general discussion with regard to the army's programme and policy. I believe my hon. friend has had his share of discussion in regard to general matters. Now he is going into various details which, it seems to me, might better be discussed under the appropriate item.
I suggest to the committee and to him, since he happened to be on his feet when I rose, that we could safely enter upon a discussion of the items themselves. I am sure hon. members of the committee will find ample opportunity to discuss any cases with respect to the administration of which the army is responsible. I think we shall get along more regularly and make better progress if the committee will enable me to do that. If that is agreed, I can now table a statement which gives a comparison with 1942-43 of the various items which have already been set out in Hansard. I suggest that we enter upon a discussion of those items. This does not shut out my hon. friend at all from dealing with the matter he has in mind when he comes to the proper item.

Speaking to the point of order, I will tell you, sir, one thing. The matter is so mixed up that we have to make quotations. I remember the minister stating that

the procedure of the committee would be as he has just indicated, but on the other hand I wonder why the discussion is so restricted precisely when the member for Temiscouata has the floor. Why was that not done when the first question was put to the minister after he had concluded his statement several days ago?

The reason is that my hon. friend is taking just twice the time taken by any other member of the committee. I thought that having had an opportunity of speaking for eighty minutes instead of forty minutes he might agree that this was the desirable thing to do. I am still speaking to the point of order. I submit that my hon. friend is not in order in discussing postponements under the national selective service regulations when we are dealing with the administration of the army. I think my hon. friend will agree with that. If he does, then the other point comes up. I made the suggestion when I was discussing the point of order that there would be ample opportunity to discuss anything in the estimates of the army.

I had the floor and I was talking to the point' of order, and strictly to the point of order. No member has the right to speak twice. The minister interrupted me and spoke twice on the point of order, and in violation of the rules he made his observations.
I answered a question.

The minister has no right to speak twice to the point of order. He has made his case and I want to make mine. I am not discussing army matters; I am discussing the application of the rules of the house to the present discussion. As a member of parliament I have protested several times against the shameless division of the tremendous amounts we are called upon to vote. I registered my solemn protest against there being only eleven items for an amount totalling nearly $1,800,000,000. How can a member of parliament stick to the subject matter when the average amount of each item is from three to five hundred million dollars? To do so creates embarrassment for you, sir; it creates embarrassment for us, and finally it creates embarrassment for the minister. It reminds me of the time when the chairman of the civil service commission and other officers were appearing before a committee to make what they called a presentation. The question is not to have a presentation; it is to have these estimates prepared as carefully as the estimates are prepared for the congress of the United States where much larger sums are voted. How can a member stick to one item when it involves such formidable amounts?

It should be much easier to do so with larger amounts than with smaller amounts.

Oh, no. The minister has just returned from Washington, and no doubt he has seen the telephone directories of New York city. The estimates tabled by President Roosevelt in congress make up a volume much larger than the telephone directories of New York city put together. I cannot understand why such a procedure is not followed here.
This is not to the point of order, I submit.
It is impossible to know when it is the right time to speak about a definite item.

speechtext: Before I rule on the point of order, may I say that the hon. member has spoken for more than forty minutes, and I have allowed him seven minutes for interruptions.
When there is an interruption I have the right to speak for another forty minutes. That is my right. The minister disputes my unquestionable right. He is a fascist.

speechtext: No one is denying any right to anyone. It is not in the mind of any member of this committee to deprive any other member of his right. There is an item of
$8,000,000 for civil salaries and wages, and it is the civilian employees who intervene in making decisions regarding the farmers. Most of them are retired from the army; they are drawing pensions, but they are the ones who make the decisions. There are a number who wear uniforms but who have never been in any theatre of war, and yet they make the decision, to send farmers and farmers' sons to the different theatres of war, to take them away from their farms. account. I cannot see any special [DOT]eason at the moment why we should' ask for i more detailed explanation of these figures. Jnless it is absolutely necessary I do not think we should take up additional time of the busy men in the national defence department.
The committee have, of course, the right to ask for it at any time.
Quite so.

Down in this corner it is doubtful when one can say anything. I agree with the minister that it is desirable at this

War Appropriation-Army
time to go into the matter of his estimates as specifically as possible, but it is unfortunate that that ruling is not enforced from his side of the house, because most of the time occupied in general statements has been spent by hon. members opposite.
No; my hon. friend is wrong about that. I believe there have been only two speeches from our side, or, counting the hon. member for Temiscouata, who made two, there have been four.

He occupied eighty minutes to-day, which is not bad for one man, and he sits on the minister's side of the house. However, I agree with the minister as to the way in which the business should be carried on. My remarks are not going to be extensive. The things I have to say are of a general nature, in an endeavour to bring to the minister's attention matters which are of an administrative character and could be handled by his department, details with which perhaps he is not familiar, for I know it is not possible for the minister to keep his finger on the many ramifications which are involved in his department.
The hori. member for Weyburn stated very fairly the position of this group with respect to military matters of an international nature. Before I proceed to bring specific matters to the attention of the minister, I should like to say, in the interest of fairness, that having listened to a good deal of criticism from both sides respecting military matters generally, I look back to 1940, w'hen I first took my seat in this house, and I do not envy any of the heads of the defence departments who accepted at that time the responsibility of organizing Canada on a military basis. The ministers faced a terrific job, with many difficulties to overcome; and, looking back to that time and seeing what they have done, I am prepared to say that they have done an excellent job of organizing Canada from a military point of view.
I wish to pay tribute to one member of the Department of National Defence to-night. If I were awarding medals for meritorious service and devotion to duty, I would have no hesitation in awarding one to the private secretary of the Minister of National Defence. There is one person who is doing an excellent job, performing 100 per cent service. Personally I can say that every matter I have brought to her attention has been handled expeditiously and satisfactorily in accordance with the regulations as they are laid down.
There is an organization under the Department of National Defence which appears to be very little known in the house; at any rate very few hon. members have made reference to it. I had the pleasure last summer of visiting North Bay and looking round a camp there. It is an edricational training school, where young men from across Canada who went into the military forces without the advantage of an education, having been weeded out, are concentrated and educated. I pay tribute to the men who organized that school and who have been administering it for the past two years. They are doing excellently an important work which in my opinion should1 be extended in the aftermath of the war. It is one which was wholly neglected before the outbreak of the present war.
I was surprised to hear the hon. member for York West state that a member of this committee proposed to take the trainees who are in Canada at the present time and send them to Alaska in order to make available the United States forces for military sendee elsewhere. I cannot suppose that anyone here would seriously suggest that, because I do not think there is any necessity for it. I believe that, of the men who are called up under the mobilization bill and have seen fit to remain in Canada, ninety-nine per cent would voluntarily cross the ocean and help their comrades in arms on the other side if the Canadian army went into action and the necessity arose for reinforcements overseas. I think it is a reflection on these boys for anyone in this house or outside it to suggest that they should remain in a certain section of Canada in order to relieve the troops of another country to cross the sea and fight somewhere else. I believe that most of these boys are in Canada as a result of lack of organization and of the proper approach. I think when the time comes and they feel it is necessary, and the parliament of this country calls on them, they will gladly cross the ocean and take their part on the other side.
I also wish to make a few observations on the proposal to split up the Canadian army. I do not know who is responsible for holding it intact in England to be used at some time in the future as a unit for whatever purpose may be designated by the military authorities. I commend the person responsible for that, whoever he may be, because I think .it is a move in the right direction. That unit could not be split up under any circumstances. Having had a little military experience, I know it is absolutely essential, and if the Canadian army, artillery and air force can work together as a unit, in the event of their going into
2974
War Appropriation-Army

action, it would be the greatest morale booster for them in action, to know that their own auxiliary forces are behind them.
There is one grievance I wish to bring to the minister's attention regarding the old soldiers' veterans guard in Canada who are performing essential service, men who went through the last war, many of whom are not in any condition to be discharging the duties they are discharging at the present time. They are essential because they have released thousands of younger men for the forces who might proceed overseas. The veterans guard when first mobilized were given to understand, I believe, that they would be utilized as far as possible in their own provinces. That has not been done. There are men from the maritimes in Ontario and vice versa. This places the men at a great disadvantage. In several letters I have received from them they complain that men from Nova Scotia are in Ontario, and they are entitled to a 48-hour leave once a month, but they are not in a position to take it and have nowhere to go. If an emergency arises and they are obliged to go to their own homes, it costs them approximately S40 to get from Ontario to Nova Scotia and vice versa. These men have families.

I do not know where my hon. friend got the idea with regard to any assurance given the veterans' guard that they would be employed in their own provinces. I have never heard of it, and I am quite satisfied that the offer of the veterans, which was certainly most enthusiastic and pressing at that time, was that they wanted to serve anywhere and preferably overseas-and they would be separated from their families more than they are now. I shall certainly inquire into that, but apart from that I want to point out that the veterans' guard is composed of about
10,000	now; 7,000 or more are employed in the administration of the prisoners of war camps, and they would have to serve where those camps are. That would present a difficulty in the way of confining their employment to their particular provinces.

I appreciate that there are administrative difficulties. The information came to me from a number of the veterans' guard themselves, particularly from Graven-hurst, where there are a considerable number of Nova Scotians. I understand that the department has made some transfers. I also agree with the minister that most of these men would like to serve overseas, where possible; but where they are subject to service in Canada, many of them were given to understand that such service would be performed, as far as possible, in their own provinces.

There may be many of them not abroad, but there are many who are. I suggest to the minister that where it is possible that arrangement should be made. Where men make application and set out extenuating circumstances to show why they should be as near as possible to their families, some consideration should be given them.
They also point out that, in the 48-hour leaves they get, a considerable amount of money is wasted because they cannot get home. That money is thrown away, whereas, if they had a furlough every so often, by means of which they could get home at a reasonable cost, they wrnuld save that money, and it would serve some useful purpose in their homes.
That is the line of argument given by the men themselves, and I have letters to that effect.
Another outstanding grievance is the matter of free pass on the railway for men on furlough or on embarkation leave. That has been brought up in the house many times. The average man going into the army to-day gets no more leave than that; that is about all he will get between the time he enlists and the time he goes overseas. He may get a furlough the first six months; his next leave is embarkation; and the soldier in the rank and file, on his present pay, if he is obliged, to go from Petawawa, or from any of the central camps in Ontario, to Nova Scotia or Saskatchewan or Manitoba, has to spend three or four months' pay which has been religiously saved if he hopes to get anywhere near meeting the cost of transportation. It is not too much to ask for free transportation for these two leaves.
Another matter that causes a great deal of concern is this, and I bring it to the minister's attention because it is responsible for much irritation. You may talk as much as you like about building the morale of the army, but you will not build it from the top or With propaganda or flowery language. You must build it up from the bottom. These things that cause irritation must be cured, and then the morale of the army will take care of itself. It is the small things that go unnoticed that irritate the rank and file and cause trouble, absenteeism and many infractions of the King's Regulations and Orders, which otherwise would not occur. The matter of stopping dependents' allowance for the wife and family in Canada of the men who go absent is something that causes trouble. That has been taken care of to some extent. The department now permits the extension of dependent's allowance up to six months. If after six months the man is still absent without leave, the dependent's allowance is cut off. There are

War Appropriation-Army
many cases where this works considerable hardship on the family in Canada. It is a problem for the woman with three or four of
a family to receive notification from the department that on a certain date her allowance will be discontinued. She is waiting and worrying for that time to arrive; it does arrive, and she receives notice that at the end of the month her allowance is discontinued. She is then in this position. Under the regulations to-day the merchant is not permitted to carry the family beyond the regular pay period; and if it is monthly, at the end of the month the grocer 'has to shut her off and she finds herself in the middle of the road with nothing. That is an embarrassing position for a woman with a family, and it does happen from time to time. I call attention to this because I think it should be taken care of. The man who commits an infraction of the military laws and is under the jurisdiction of the sergeant-major should pay the penalty, and not his family, and where the wife's allowance is discontinued it is the family that is penalized. But he is taken care of if he is in the guard room, because he has no worries about where he is to get something to eat.
Another thing that causes friction in Canada is the call-up. The national selective service sends a call for military training, and when it is received the man reports to the military board and comes under national defence. He is taken into service for four or five or six days and given a medical examination, and in many cases he is rejected for military service. There does not appear to be any coordination between the national defence board that rejects him and the national selective service board that calls him up. I know of instances where a man was rejected this week for military service. He went back to work with his mind free; he was not going to be taken into service because he was medically unfit and he made commitments financially. But two or three weeks later he gets a call to report back.

The procedure is this.
When the call-up comes the man may go to a local physician and ascertain whether he is physically fit. If he is physically fit, he has then to go for medical examination. He goes to the military board my hon. friend speaks of and he is still not in the army. He is examined by the board and, if rejected, he is still under national selective service. He is only examined by the board. If rejected, he is still under national selective service. My hon. friend says that there is no cooperation or coordination between the medical boards
and national selective service. I have in mind that if a man is rejected he is given a return ticket, is he not? National selective service has told me that what they do is to send in the return half of the ticket, to be given to the man in case he is rejected.
In this particular case the man did not travel any distance. He reported in the city.
Was it an army medical board?
Yes.
What city?

In the city of Toronto. I know of another case in Nova Scotia where a boy was in the army for fourteen months and then discharged as medically unfit and sent home. He took employment at the naval station in Sydney and worked there for about three weeks. Then he got a call from national selective service to report for military duty.

That is another matter. Probably my hon friend has gone into it fully himself. But as I understand it, when a man is examined by a civilian doctor and is turned down, or rejected as my hon. friend says, the national selective service boards have a medical revision officer who looks over the medical report which has been made by the civilian doctor on the man who has been called up, and if that board feel that the doctor has made a mistake in classifying the man they may order him in. [DOT] I think that is what happened in the case of which my hon. friend speaks. But that again is a board under national selective service, and not under the army.

The man I mentioned was in the army for fourteen months and then discharged. But that case has been taken care of. I got in touch with the authorities at Halifax, and they informed me that the trouble was the lack of proper records, that a mistake had been made.
It sounds like a bad mistake.

The Toronto man was in the service for five or six days, and was medically examined, then given a rejection slip as being medically unfit. He was in category E. I think what the board should have done was to notify national selective service that this man had been discharged as medically unfit, but that apparently was not done because the man has since been called up twice, all within two months.	.

Is this Toronto too?
War Appropriation-Army

Yes; that is Toronto. The man was let out as medically unfit, and he understood that the army was through with him. He bought a house and involved himself in contract commitments. Then a week later he was called back in again. He just does not know where he stands. I think the board that rejected him should' notify national selective service that he is through so far as calling him for military service is concerned. It is a matter of perfecting the mechanics.
Did the hon. member chase that case down? Was it remedied?
No; it has not been remedied.
What is the man's name? Perhaps my hon. friend would give it to me afterwards.
The fact of the matter is that I was going to bring it to the attention of the minister's secretary. I find her the best fixer-upper in Ottawa.
Along with the minister.
I am interested in a man being in the army for six days and then buying a house. We must be treating him well.

He was rejected and was out for about a month when he thought he could safely undertake this commitment. I will let that matter rest there because I think it has been sufficiently discussed to be understood.
There is another matter which I have discussed in the house on several occasions. It is the case of the soldier who .adopts a child prior to enlistment. Under the regulations you cannot receive an allowance for a child you have been maintaining unless you go through the regular adoption proceedings. But there are cases where that is not possible. One case I would bring to the minister's attention is that of a man in the veterans guard. He is the grandfather of the child, who is nine years old, and has been maintaining that child. It is the child of one of his daughters. Under the regulations he cannot receive an allowance unless he adopts the child. The grandfather does not want to adopt his daughter's child. I think there should be some flexibility in administration to cover cases of that kind. You cannot make hard and fast regulations that will cover everything. There should be some latitude to cover cases of this kind and settle them on the basis of common sense. There are borderline cases, perhaps not many, but hardship is caused if there is not flexibility in the regulations. I have received many letters from different people who have told

me that it is impossible, on account of relationship, to go through the regular adoption proceedings, and there is a child suffering as a result.
The. hon. member is suggesting a dependent's allowance in the case of a child who is a blood relative but is not adopted?

That is right.
There is another matter. I have received several resolutions from religious organizations across the. country to the effect that in the camps, army, navy and air force, there is not sufficient building space to permit the different religious organizations to carry on their church services in the camp. I do not know what the actual situation is, but there seems to be some basis for the complaint because these representations are made in resolution form and come from both east and west, and from the Catholic Women's League of Canada particularly. I would' like the minister to check up on that, if possible.
There is another matter relating to the women's auxiliary services. We protest the differential in pay that exists for men's and women's services. When we appealed to the women of this country to don the uniform, it was on the basis that they would be relieving men for active service overseas or for some form of active military service that could not be done by women. When a woman gets into uniform and performs the same job as the .man she relieves was performing, I think she is entitled to the same rate of pay that he was getting. I notice that in Ottawa and other cities women are taking over the driving of ambulances, running jeeps and other vehicles, relieving men for essential military service. In such cases the differential in pay should disappear, and they are entitled to exactly the same rate as is paid the men. That also applies to trades pay. When a woman takes a job that a man was doing previous^., the same rate of pay should apply throughout the service.
Another point is that the women's auxiliary services are not entitled to dependents' allowance,. I do not think there would be very many affected; but there are cases where a girl enlists, maybe two from one family, leaving behind an old father and an old mother, not old enough to receive the old age pension, but too old to work, being between sixty and seventy years of age, and the old couple may have been absolutely dependent upon the income of the two girls. The. regulations do not permit the paying of an allowance in that case. I think the regulations should be changed to permit the

War Appropriation-Army
payment of dependents' allowance in circumstances such as that in respect of a girl who is in the service.
Another matter the minister would be well advised to check up on is the increase in pay. I think he is aware himself that there is considerable friction over this matter, not only in Canada but also overseas. The statement was made by the government that army pay would be increased to $1.50 for the soldier, and so on for non-commissioned officers up to a certain category. That has not been applied as a general increase. It was accepted as a general increase by the service and the public at large, but. in the application certain restrictions have been imposed which make it almost impossible for many men in the service to obtain the increase. For example, the administration of that order is in the hands of the commanding officer, who has complete jurisdiction. After a boy has been in the service for four months, he is entitled to apply to the commanding officer for the first ten cents a day, provided he has no crime sheet, and if he is considered an efficient soldier, and has taken the basic training. There are many men in the service, in the postal corps and many other branches, whose work did not require them to take the basic training. A number of them have been in the army for two or three years; they have not had their basic training; but in order to qualify for that increase they must go back and take basic training, though it is absolutely unnecessary in their branch of the service. Many men are writing back from overseas that though they have been in the army for three years they have not been recommended and have not received this increase. They may have committed some slight infraction of king's regulations and orders, which is considered as militating against them, so that the increase in pay is not forthcoming.
I want hon. members to stop for a moment and visualize the position of the men overseas, who have been pretty much inactive for the last three years. This situation has tended to get a number of the younger fellows into minor difficulties, such as being absent without leave, for which they have been confined to barracks. We can all understand that this is a natural reaction to the life they have been leading during the- last three years. In view of the fact that this was advertised as a general increase for the services, which was warranted at this time; in view of the fact that the whole army may be in action very shortly, I think it would be a fine gesture, as well as something absolutely merited, if the government would eliminate these stumbling blocks and restrictive measures that are
irritating thousands of our boys to-day, and as a result of which they have not received these increases. Hundreds of these young men do not understand the regulations; they do not know how to go about making theii applications, and no one takes up the matter for them. Therefore I think the minister would be well advised to do something about it now.
I am sorry I have had to take up so much time on these general matters of an administrative nature, but I wanted to leave them with the minister. There are other matters that we can perhaps discuss under his estimates.

I wonder if we could consider that we are discussing the first item, just in order to proceed as regularly as possible. I do not want to be strict in holding people down; I know that to a certain extent civil salaries and wages apply to these other items as well.. That is to say, there are civilians engaged in administering some of these services, but perhaps we might consider that we are proceeding under the item of $8,832,687.

I rise to a question of privilege as a member of the House of Commons. I protest -most solemnly because the list of these civil employees of the Department of National Defence, together with their salaries, is not given in the estimates, as it was previously. No names were given, but at least we knew there were so many positions at certain salaries. Now all we know is that eight million dollars is to be spent under this item. I contend that such an estimate is an insult to parliament.

I will try to confine my remarks to the first item, and I wish to support what was said by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) in regard to increases in pay. In checking up in Peterborough, we have not been able to find any dependent who has received any of this extra assigned pay.
Where is that?

In
Peterborough.
That really comes under item No. 2.
This document we have been given is headed *' secret." Does that mean we cannot take it away from here?
No.

Then I shall reserve my remarks until the next item.
War Appropriation-Army

I should like the minister to give us some more detailed information about the first item. The amount it is estimated will be expended1 is $8,832,687. Who receives that money? How many persons receive civil salaries and wages to that amount from the army? Do these people all reside in Canada?
Perhaps my hon. friend will let me answer one question at a time. I presume he is asking about the estimate for the coming year?
Yes.

Of course the estimate for the coming year is based on the requisitions which have been sent in by the different districts and which in turn have been gone over by the director of civilian personnel and, shall.I say, netted; the result is the estimate for the coming year. I cannot give the exact figure, but for Ottawa the estimate is permanent staff, 58; temporary staff, 2,982, or a total of 3,040. Those employed outside Ottawa are estimated as: permanent staff, 108; temporary staff, 4,318, or a total of 4,426, giving a grand total of 7,466. That is the estimate of the number who will be required this year, and is an increase of about 3,300 over last year. That increase will amount to about 1,300 in Ottawa and 2,000 outside Ottawa. That takes care not only of civilian clerks and office help, but also of caretakers, heating staff,
. engineers and all that sort of thing in the different establishments throughout the country.
That is what I wished to get from the minister. Apparently these people are paid by the army, but they are not in the army. What is the nature of their work?

I have mentioned the sort of work they do, and here are some of the branches in which they work in the militia services here in Ottawa; the branches of the C.G.S., the adjutant general, the M.G.O. and1 the quartermaster general, all have civilian staffs. I think the number of permanent employees there is something like sixty. Then there are the miscellaneous services, which are principally in Ottawa and include subdivisions of the military branches, and the directorate of public relations. Then outside Ottawa, in the different military districts, in addition to clerical assistants and storemen, and people of that kind, these employees would be mostly engineers and people having to do with the administration and servicing of the different establishments.
The 5,000 are outside Ottawa; are any of them outside Canada?
I understand there are 400 in the United Kingdom.
None in the United States?
Very few in the United States. Possibly some in connection with the military attache.
The minister mentioned some being employed in public relations. What are their duties?

The branch of the director of information has to do with contact with the press, the radio and with films. He handles matters of publicity, and the gathering of information. They are stationed in the different districts. Possibly the hon. member will know Colonel Jennings in Saint John, who was formerly with the Telegraph-Journal. They have a certain amount of civilian staff under them. He is in charge of information for the army.

Is there any connection
between them and the wartime information board?

No, no functional connection. One does not take orders from the other. But there is coordination in that the directors of public relations in the different branches and different departments do meet at stated times with the wartime information board in order to coordinate the dissemination of information, and the collection and compilation of information for the public.

How many people are employed in the public relations branch, and
what are their salaries?
I cannot tell my hon. friend offhand. It is mostly military personnel.

The minister mentioned
Colonel Jennings. He wears a uniform and has, I think, the rank of lieutenant-colonel. He was a newspaperman, and stepped into the army a few months ago with the rank of lieutenant-colonel. I believe he saw service in the last war.
Yes.
But, with his uniform, he would not be classified as civilian personnel?
No; he would not.

He would not be included in that item.

War Appropriation-Army

No; the hon. member asked about the work which was done, and I was simply stating who was in charge of it. I said there was a certain number of civilian personnel, but that in connection with the director of public relations they are mostly military.
Why is there an increase of $3,500,000 this year?

All I can tell my hon. friend is that there are increased activities all across Canada, and that these requisitions have come in from the different districts. There are some, of course, doing away with military personnel, and using civilian personnel. All I can say is that this is simply an estimate. As a request for an appointment comes in, it is looked into first by the deputy minister, and afterwards by a representative of the civil service commission, who must examine the representations put forward as to the necessity for employment, and who certifies, or otherwise, as to whether or not employment should be given. This is making a provision for employees who will not actually be employed until the civil service commission has certified that their employment is necessary.
And that will be $3,500,000 extra.

With regard to this item, in my humble view all civilians should be under it. When I speak of civilians I speak of those who wear the uniform, without having gained any experience in any theatre of war, but who are here at headquarters. I have one in mind, a district magistrate, who was gazetted as a captain or a major, and who is now a lieutenant-colonel. He was just a district magistrate or recorder here in Ottawa. Because he has been transferred to the branch of the judge advocate-general he has become what we call in French un foudre de guerre-a thunderbolt.
How is it, sir, that here in Ottawa we see many fellows who are very strict as to their uniforms, who are the Beau Brummels of the town, and who rise in military rank without gaining any further military experience.
I say to my hon. friend that they are not included in this item.

I will speak about them in due course. I will come back to the farmers then. Here is the case of one fellow
-and I do not wish ,to put it over you, Mr. Chairman; I have too much respect for the Chair to do that. .

speechtext: Order. I believe the minister has said that the subject of farmers comes under the Department of Labour.

No; the farmer is in the
army.

speechtext: We are discussing the first item in the summary.
The minister stated he had no objection to discussing the cases of farmers who are in the army, provided that we leave aside the mobilization board.
No; I said I had no objection to the matter being discussed under the appropriate item, and in my judgment the appropriate item would foe the next one on the list, namely, pay and allowances.

Yes; but now, sir, I will say something about that. With great respect, many people who look after the soldiers, after they are in the arniy, are paid by virtue of this item. Therefore, because they have their word to say with respect to the draftees being kept in the army or being granted leave, I submit that the farmers come under this item.

I know, or at least I think I know that my hon. friend does not wish to make just a hollow sham of what the committee is endeavouring to do, with the full consent of the house. And it would be making a hollow sham of it if he continued his discussion under this item, when there is an item, No. 2 on the list, under which the subject could be properly discussed. It is no doubt true that there may be some stenographer who probably has written a letter to some soldier who possibly may have been a farmer; but this is not the proper item under which we should discuss a substantive case such as my hon. friend is about to bring up.
I say again to my hon. friend that he is an old parliamentarian, and I do not know whether or not he wishes to be the bad boy of the party, but I suggest to him that he should discuss the matter under item No. 2, the proper one, and not under item No. 1.

That is exactly what I
have said. I have asked repeatedly for a list of these men who received pay under this item, and the answer that has been given to

War Appropriation-Army

the hon. member for St. John-Albert is as clear as mud. I am surprised that the hon. member is satisfied with it.
You got up ahead of me.

He is very generous. Here we have an item amounting to 88,832,000, or about 83,500,000 more than last year. Why? Because this year we shall have more to do. Is that the reason? Who are those who are to be employed this year, who were not employed last year?

I have said that I do
not see how in the world I can give the names of people who are not yet employed. I have said that this was an estimate to provide for the employment of people if the civil service commission, when application is made for their employment, authorizes the employment. Until that comes about, we cannot give the names.
Here again the civil service commission is the smoke-screen. Have you any information about the $5,300,000 last year? The answer I get is, "No, sir."
Have you asked for it?

No, I did not ask for it. We have the expenditures for last year and the estimates for this year. The fiscal year has been ended for nearly two months, and we do not have the precise figures with regard to the expenditures of last year. It is not so much a question of dollars and cents, or finding the fraction of a cent regarding the amount paid to anyone; what we want is who these people are, what they are doing and -how much they are paid. That should be easy to get. Why have we been refused that? Why is the Department of National Defence hiding information from members of parliament?

That has never been
asked from any department under any peacetime estimate, so that I do not know what my hon. friend means when he says we are hiding it. If my hon. friend wants me to give him a list of the people drawing salaries to the total amount of 85,300,000, I suppose it could be done, but it would take a good deal of time and I do not think the committee would expect me to do it.

What about the billion
dollars the government is giving away to other countries?

speechtext:
I do not see how the
billion dollars has anything to do with this item. I must ask the hon. member to keep

within the item so that we may get ahead with the work of the committee. It is
absolutely impossible to make any headway the present way.

I am not insisting on that, but when the minister says that no one has asked for the names of those who have been employed under this item he should remember the numerous questions I asked1, some of which were answered and some of which were not. He must remember that I asked the Prime Minister a question about the whole civil service, and he said he would improve the public accounts in order to give me that information. I asked the Minister of Finance for that information, and he said it would take too long to give it to me. Let us look at the future. Let us look at the estimates for this year. We are to provide $8,800,000 for civil service salaries and wages. The minister says that these men will be appointed by the civil service commission. Can he give us a pledge that no man will be appointed under this item by order in council? Can he give us an idea of the number of people who were appointed last year by order in council under this particular item instead of by the civil service commission? This information is given in the United States and in England. It must be given in China because the Chinese are sensible and they want to do things well. It is probably given by Joe Stalin in Russia. I am not sure about China and Russia, but I presume that they do it because they do things well. We want to know how many men will be appointed and to what positions. Perhaps the appointments have not yet been made, but I presume the minister can give an approximate idea. Can he inform us who will be appointed and what will they do? Will he take only physical unfits for these jobs?
The provisions of P.C.4759 will be adhered to. That order in council provides that men are not taken if they are physically fit.
I ask the minister kindly to table a copy of that order in council to-morrow so that we can read it.
It has been tabled already.
The members have not been supplied with it.
That is under the War Measures Act.

There are many things we do not see, especially the order in council which appointed the minister perpetual acting Minister of Finance.

Passports
The order in council has been tabled and the hon. member can see it.
I will get it. I wonder if the order in council gives only a direction to the civil service commission, or "will it govern all future appointments by order in council.
Read it and find out.

That is a fine way to get out of it. I want to know what these positions are. The minister says that nobody has asked for these names. Does he not remember that last year I produced a copy of the budget of the United States as an example. The Minister of National Defence may suffer from amnesia, but the other members of this committee do not.

Surely the hon. member does not mean the implication he has made against the minister. I ask that he follow standing order 58 and keep within the item. The personal condition of the minister has nothing to do with the item before the committee at the present time.
